name: using-superpowers
description: Use when starting any conversation - establishes how to find and use skills, requiring skill invocation before ANY response including clarifying questions
---

<SUBAGENT-STOP>
If you were dispatched as a subagent to execute a specific task, ignore this skill.
</SUBAGENT-STOP>

<EXTREMELY-IMPORTANT>
If you think there is even a 1% chance a skill might apply to what you are doing, you ABSOLUTELY MUST invoke the skill.

IF A SKILL APPLIES TO YOUR TASK, YOU DO NOT HAVE A CHOICE. YOU MUST USE IT.

This is not negotiable. You cannot rationalize your way out of this.
</EXTREMELY-IMPORTANT>

## The Rule

**Invoke relevant or requested skills BEFORE any response or action** — including clarifying questions, exploring the codebase, or checking files. If it turns out wrong for the situation, you don't have to use it.

**Before entering plan mode:** if you haven't already brainstormed, invoke the brainstorming skill first.

Then announce "Using [skill] to [purpose]" and follow the skill exactly. If it has a checklist, create a todo per item.

## Skill Priority

When multiple skills apply, process skills come first — they set the approach, then implementation skills (frontend-design, etc.) carry it out. Brainstorming and systematic-debugging are Superpowers' most common process skills, but the rule holds for any of them.

- "Let's build X" → superpowers:brainstorming first, then implementation skills.
- "Fix this bug" → superpowers:systematic-debugging first, then domain skills.

## Red Flags

These thoughts mean STOP—you're rationalizing:

| Thought | Reality |
|---------|---------|
| "This is just a simple question" | Questions are tasks. Check for skills. |
| "I need more context first" | Skill check comes BEFORE clarifying questions. |
| "Let me explore the codebase first" | Skills tell you HOW to explore. Check first. |
| "I can check git/files quickly" | Files lack conversation context. Check for skills. |
| "Let me gather information first" | Skills tell you HOW to gather information. |
| "This doesn't need a formal skill" | If a skill exists, use it. |
| "I remember this skill" | Skills evolve. Read current version. |
| "This doesn't count as a task" | Action = task. Check for skills. |
| "The skill is overkill" | Simple things become complex. Use it. |
| "I'll just do this one thing first" | Check BEFORE doing anything. |
| "This feels productive" | Undisciplined action wastes time. Skills prevent this. |
| "I know what that means" | Knowing the concept ≠ using the skill. Invoke it. |

## Platform Adaptation

If your harness appears here, read its reference file for special instructions:

- Codex: `references/codex-tools.md`
- Pi: `references/pi-tools.md`
- Antigravity: `references/antigravity-tools.md`

## User Instructions

User instructions (CLAUDE.md, AGENTS.md, GEMINI.md, etc, direct requests) take precedence over skills, which in turn override default behavior. Only skip skill workflows or instructions when your human partner has explicitly told you to.
</EXTREMELY_IMPORTANT>"

## The Rule

**Invoke relevant or requested skills BEFORE any response or action** — including clarifying questions, exploring the codebase, or checking files. If it turns out wrong for the situation, you don't have to use it.

**Before entering plan mode:** if you haven't already brainstormed, invoke the brainstorming skill first.

Then announce "Using [skill] to [purpose]" and follow the skill exactly. If it has a checklist, create a todo per item.

## Skill Priority

When multiple skills apply, process skills come first — they set the approach, then implementation skills (frontend-design, etc.) carry it out. Brainstorming and systematic-debugging are Superpowers' most common process skills, but the rule holds for any of them.

- "Let's build X" → superpowers:brainstorming first, then implementation skills.
- "Fix this bug" → superpowers:systematic-debugging first, then domain skills.

## Red Flags

These thoughts mean STOP—you're rationalizing:

| Thought | Reality |
|---------|---------|
| "This is just a simple question" | Questions are tasks. Check for skills. |
| "I need more context first" | Skill check comes BEFORE clarifying questions. |
| "Let me explore the codebase first" | Skills tell you HOW to explore. Check first. |
| "I can check git/files quickly" | Files lack conversation context. Check for skills. |
| "Let me gather information first" | Skills tell you HOW to gather information. |
| "This doesn't need a formal skill" | If a skill exists, use it. |
| "I remember this skill" | Skills evolve. Read current version. |
| "This doesn't count as a task" | Action = task. Check for skills. |
| "The skill is overkill" | Simple things become complex. Use it. |
| "I'll just do this one thing first" | Check BEFORE doing anything. |
| "This feels productive" | Undisciplined action wastes time. Skills prevent this. |
| "I know what that means" | Knowing the concept ≠ using the skill. Invoke it. |

# Free vs Pro — what we charge for, and why

_Decided 2026-07-24. This is the record; if the code disagrees, the code is wrong._

The only prior written record of the commercial model is the design itself, twice
(`Fitcheck.dc.html:698`, `:797`):

> **Go Pro · £5/mo** — *"Unlimited daily looks, packing mode & cost-per-wear analytics."*

> ⚠️ **The price is €5/mo, not £5** (decided 2026-08-05). The quote above is the design verbatim and is
> left intact as the citation it is, but **£ was a design-file artefact**: the app targets the EU, Supabase
> is EU-region, and every price already renders in euro (`lib/closet/wear-stats.ts` uses `en-IE` /
> `currency: "EUR"`). A Pro card reading £5 on a screen where cost-per-wear reads €3.00 is a visible
> inconsistency. **`2026-07-24-profile-hub.md` instructs "render that copy verbatim" — that instruction is
> superseded for the price only;** the feature list still ships verbatim.

Three features. This document expands that into a full tier definition, keeps it consistent with
**Decision 4** in `CLAUDE.md` — *"the free tier must stay genuinely great — consumer apps die when the
paywall hits before the magic moment"* — and checks it against what we actually pay to serve.

---

## 1. The principle: meter what costs us money, sell what compounds

Two different things can justify a price, and confusing them is how apps end up gating their own growth.

- **Cost-to-serve.** Every AI generation costs real money. That is a *meter*, and metering it is honest.
- **Compounding value.** Analytics, planning, advice. Zero marginal cost, high willingness to pay,
  and — importantly — *worthless to a new user*. Nobody pays for cost-per-wear on day one; they pay for
  it in month three, once the data is theirs.

Everything else stays free. In particular, three things must **never** be gated:

| Never gate | Why |
|---|---|
| **The daily drop + the "why"** | It is the product. Gating it means nobody discovers the magic. |
| **The Style DNA share card** | It is a growth channel, not a feature. Charging for your own marketing is self-harm. |
| **Tagging, item editing, and the closet's *quality*** | The closet is the moat and the switching cost. Every item added makes the product better *and* makes leaving harder. **Amended 2026-08-05:** a generous SIZE cap (50, see §2) is now in place, but nothing about how a closet works is gated — no reduced tagging, no locked fields, no degraded stylist. The cap is a ceiling on quantity, never on capability. |

---

## 2. The meter: three rerolls a day

> **AMENDED 2026-08-04.** This section previously read *"Free gets 3 AI generations per day"*, counting
> the daily drop toward that three. **It contradicted §1 of this same document**, which says the daily
> drop must never be gated — with drops counted, a free user who has viewed three occasions is refused
> the fourth, which is precisely gating the drop. §1 is what matches Decision 4 in `CLAUDE.md`, so §2 is
> the part that gave. The old wording is also what `2026-07-22-regenerate-quota.md` disagreed with; all
> three documents now say the same thing.

**Every occasion's first look of the day is free, on every tier. Free gets three rerolls a day, pooled
across all occasions. Pro rerolls without limit.**

> **Pooled, not per-occasion** (decided 2026-08-05). A per-occasion allowance was built first and
> reverted: most people care about ONE occasion on a given day, so rationing per occasion is strictest
> exactly where attention goes and generous where nobody is looking — you could be refused a second Work
> reroll while holding an unused Evening one you never wanted. The usual objection to a shared pool, that
> it can block an occasion you have not opened, **does not apply once drops are free**: tapping a new
> occasion is always a drop, so the pool only ever meters rerolls.

A "generation" is any call that spends a model request. There are three kinds, and they are metered
differently:

| Kind | Free | Pro |
|---|---|---|
| **`drop`** — an occasion's first look of the day | Always free | Always free |
| **`regenerate`** — asking an occasion again | 3 per day, all occasions | Unlimited |
| **`styled`** — building a look around a chosen piece | Gated (Pro #2) | Unlimited |

Reading a look that already exists is always free and always unlimited, per Decision 5 — including
re-opening a styled look, which is cached per (user, item, local day).

The limit bites at the honest moment: someone rerolling a third time is genuinely dissatisfied, which is
when "Pro rerolls without limit" is a fair offer rather than a toll.

**No counter is displayed** (decided 2026-08-05). The user is not told how many rerolls remain before
they run out. A visible "1 left" badge makes every free user think about the limit constantly, which is
the opposite of this section's design — *a user who never thinks about the limit never hits it*.

### The ceiling, which is the number that matters

Four occasion drops plus three rerolls:

```
7 × $0.003 = $0.021/day  →  $0.63/user/month absolute worst case
```

Realistic use is 2–3 generations a day, so ≈ $0.20/month. **The ceiling is the point:** a free tier needs
a worst case you can survive, and it must not scale with closet size. This is why `styled` is Pro rather
than "first time per item free" — the latter has no ceiling at all, since a 150-item closet would permit
150 free generations a day, and it would leave nothing in Pro #2 to sell.

### The arithmetic, so the number is not a vibe

Haiku 4.5 at $1/1M in, $5/1M out. One text-only re-rank ≈ 1,500 in + 300 out:

```
(1500 / 1M × $1) + (300 / 1M × $5) = $0.0015 + $0.0015 ≈ $0.003 per generation
```

| Scenario | Cost/user/month |
|---|---|
| Free user, realistic ~1.5 generations/day | **≈ $0.14** |
| Free user maxing the ceiling — 7/day | **≈ $0.63** |
| Pro user, heavy — 10/day | **≈ $0.90** (vs €5 revenue) |

Item tagging is one-time and negligible: a 100-item closet is ~$0.20, ever.

### Closet size: 50 pieces free (decided 2026-08-05)

**A free closet holds 50 pieces. Pro is unlimited.**

A 10-per-day rate limit was built first and removed in favour of this: with a ceiling in place the rate
was redundant, and two overlapping rules made the free tier feel meaner than it is — a new user would
have needed five days to reach 50, throttled during exactly the days you want them filling their closet.
One rule is easier to explain and easier to sell against.

**The cap counts UNARCHIVED pieces.** Nothing in the product deletes an item, so counting archived ones
would strand a user at the cap with no way back under it. Archiving is the intended way to make room,
and an archived piece is not in your closet by any reading of the word.

This section previously read *"Do not cap closet size"* full stop. What survives of that reasoning, and
why **50** rather than a tighter number:

- **Storage does not justify a total cap.** Measured on the real local closet: `original.jpg` averages
  233 kB and `cutout.webp` 97 kB, so **330 kB per item**. A 100-item closet is 33 MB; 10,000 free users
  with full closets is ~330 GB, about **$4.83/month**. The far bigger lever is queue #13
  `cutout-backfill` — 10 legacy `cutout.png` files still average ~700 kB, 7× their WebP equivalent.
- **A LOW cap would degrade the product rather than gate it.** PR #15 measured a 21-item closet at **21
  combos in winter against 48 in summer**; PR #14 exists because small closets starve the candidate
  pool. Cap items at 20–30 and free users judge the stylist on a wardrobe too thin for it to work —
  selling a worse magic moment rather than fewer features. **50 sits clear of that range**, so a free
  closet is a full one with a ceiling, not a starved one.
- §1's reasoning still holds directionally: the closet is the moat and the switching cost, which is why
  the cap is generous rather than the 20-ish figure common in this category.

The limit is enforced in `uploadAndTag`, not `confirmItem`: the two storage writes and the tagging call
all happen before the confirm screen, so a check at confirm would already have paid for the item it
refuses.

At 5% conversion, 100 users cost roughly $14–27/month to serve and return ~€25. Thin but positive — and
Pro users are cheap to serve relative to what they pay, which is the right shape. **If real usage runs
above ~2 generations/day for free users, lower the free allowance to 2 before raising the price.**

---

## 3. The tiers

### Free — the whole loop, forever

- **Up to 50 closet pieces** (unarchived), with full AI tagging, background removal and item editing —
  the cap is on quantity, never on capability
- The daily drop: **every** occasion's looks with the one-sentence why, never rationed
- **3 rerolls per day**, pooled across all occasions
- Per-item wear facts on the item detail screen (times worn, cost-per-wear, last worn) — the *screen*
  that analyses the whole wardrobe is Pro #4; a fact about the piece you are looking at is not
- Wear logging, the Fit Diary, streaks — *the habit loop is what creates a payer*
- Style DNA card and sharing
- Up to **10 saved outfits**
- Weather, location, rain guard, all preferences

### Pro — €5/mo

| # | Feature | Type | Source |
|---|---|---|---|
| # | Feature | Type | Source |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | **Unlimited rerolls** — reroll freely, any occasion | Meter | Design (*"unlimited daily looks"*) |
| 2 | **Style an outfit with this** — build a look around any piece, unlimited | Meter | New |
| 3 | **Packing mode** — a trip in, a capsule and per-day looks out | Meter + planning | Design |
| 4 | **Cost-per-wear analytics** — the full Wear Stats screen | Compounding | Design |
| 5 | **Gap analysis** — *"a camel overcoat unlocks 14 new outfits"* | Compounding | New |
| 6 | **Unlimited saved outfits + favourites** | Compounding | New |
| 7 | **Unlimited closet size** — past the free 50 | Ceiling | New (2026-08-05) |
| 8 | **3D avatar** — see your looks on a body, not a flat-lay | Compounding + meter | New (2026-08-12), **not costed** |

Items 1, 3 and 4 are the design's own three. The rest are what turn them into a bundle worth a recurring
charge rather than a single metered button.

> **Packing mode is advertised before it exists, deliberately** (user, 2026-08-05). The entitlement
> (`packingMode`) and the pitch copy both name it; the feature is scoping-only
> (`plans/scoping/2026-07-24-packing-mode-scoping.md`, seven open decisions). This is acceptable **while
> in development and while nobody can pay** — no checkout exists. ⚠️ **It must be built before Pro is
> actually sold**, or the copy has to drop it: charging for a named feature that does not exist is the
> one version of this that is not acceptable.

### 3D avatar — added 2026-08-12, and it CANNOT be costed yet

The strongest Pro feature on this list in principle: a flat-lay tells you the pieces go together, an
avatar tells you whether they suit *you*. It is also the only feature here that could plausibly justify
a price above €5, and the only one a competitor cannot copy in an afternoon.

**It is deliberately entered with no number against it**, because the cost swings by two orders of
magnitude on decisions nobody has made:

| Decision | Cheap end | Expensive end |
|---|---|---|
| **The body** | One parametric avatar from a few measurements, built once per user, reused forever | Photogrammetry from user photos, rebuilt whenever they change |
| **The garments** | 2D cutouts warped onto the avatar — no 3D asset at all | A 3D mesh per garment, generated per item at capture |
| **When it renders** | Client-side, in the browser, on demand | Server-side render per look, per day |
| **Who pays for compute** | The device | Us, per view |

The cheap combination is close to free per user after a one-time avatar build. The expensive one is a
per-garment generation cost on top of a per-view render cost, which scales with closet size *and*
engagement — the exact shape §2 rejected for `styled` ("no ceiling at all").

**Before this can enter a break-even model it needs, in order:**

1. A brainstorm and a scoping doc, like packing mode and the stylist chat have.
2. **A measured cost per avatar and per garment**, not an estimate — the same discipline the $0.003
   generation figure came from.
3. A decision on whether it is inside €5 or the reason a second, higher tier exists.

⚠️ **Do not put it in the Pro marketing copy until it exists.** Packing mode is already being advertised
before it is built, which is acceptable only while nothing can be bought. Two such features would make
the pitch mostly fiction.

### Why gap analysis is the sharpest one

It is the only feature that answers *"what should I buy?"* — the highest-intent question a wardrobe app
can be asked. It is also the natural home for the design's **"See curated picks"** CTA (`:767`), which
makes it the bridge to a second revenue line. It is deliberately Pro from day one so that affiliate
revenue never becomes a reason to degrade the free experience.

### Why packing mode earns its place

It is the only Pro feature with a hard deadline attached — you need it *this week, before the flight* —
which converts far better than an open-ended benefit. It is episodic, so it does not inflate steady-state
cost, and it is the most screenshot-shareable output the product could produce.

**Packing mode does not exist in any spec, design or plan.** It needs a brainstorm before a plan; see §5.

---

## 4. What this means for the code

**Everything Pro must route through one seam.** Gating six screens by retrofitting `if (isPro)` into
each is how this becomes unmaintainable — and it is exactly the fork where this project's stated
preference is the extensible option, not the minimal diff.

`lib/outfits/quota.ts` is already that seam for generations (`assertCanGenerate` currently returns
unconditionally). It needs to widen into `lib/billing/entitlements.ts` covering both meters and
capabilities:

```ts
type Entitlements = {
  tier: Tier;
  /** Per occasion, per day. null = unlimited. Drops themselves are never metered. */
  regeneratesPerOccasion: number | null;
  /** "Style an outfit with this" — Pro #2. */
  styledLooks: boolean;
  savedOutfits: number | null;
  analytics: boolean;                 // the Wear Stats SCREEN, not the item tile
  gapAnalysis: boolean;
  packingMode: boolean;
};
```

> **AMENDED 2026-08-04:** this was `generationsPerDay: number | null`, matching the superseded §2. A
> single daily number cannot express "drops are always free, regenerates are capped per occasion", and
> counting stored `outfits` rows cannot implement it either — a regenerate *replaces* the day's rows for
> an occasion, so afterwards a first drop and a fifth are indistinguishable. Hence the
> `generation_events` ledger, pulled forward from `2026-07-22-regenerate-quota.md`.

Two hard rules:

1. **"Limited" is a state, not an error.** A user at their daily limit sees an explanation and an
   upgrade path, never a thrown exception or a blank screen. This is already the stated design of the
   regenerate-quota plan; it now applies everywhere.
2. **Read entitlements server-side only.** A client-side check is a suggestion.

Until billing exists, `entitlements()` returns the free tier for everyone, with a local override so Pro
surfaces can be built and tested. **No Stripe until the features are worth paying for.**

## 6. Not yet tiered

- **Talk to the stylist** (`plans/scoping/2026-07-24-stylist-chat-scoping.md`) — free-text intent
  ("outdoor wedding, 28°") or an actual chat. Which tier it lands in depends entirely on which of those
  two it is: one-shot intent extraction costs about **a third of a generation** and fits inside the free
  3/day meter; a multi-turn conversation resends its history every turn, so cost grows quadratically and
  it would have to be **Pro and turn-capped**. Decide the feature before deciding its tier.

## 7. What a break-even model needs, and what this document was missing

_Added 2026-08-12, when a break-even model was first asked for._

**Sections 1–4 model COST-TO-SERVE, not a business.** They answer "what does an AI generation cost", and
they answer it well and by measurement. A break-even model needs three more things this document did not
have: what actually reaches the bank from €5, the infrastructure that is not AI, and the fixed costs
that exist whether anyone subscribes or not.

### 7.1 €5 is not €5 — roughly €3.84 reaches us

Verified against Stripe's published EEA pricing, 2026-08-12:

| Line | On a €5/mo subscription |
|---|---|
| Gross | €5.00 |
| **VAT** (EU digital services, OSS — 19% DE, 17% LU … 27% HU) | **−€0.80** if the price is VAT-INCLUSIVE |
| **Stripe**, EEA standard card — 1.5% + €0.25 | −€0.33 |
| **Stripe Billing** — 0.7% of volume | −€0.04 |
| **Net** | **≈ €3.84** |

That is a **23% haircut**, and two things inside it deserve attention:

- **The €0.25 fixed fee is 5% on its own at this price**, before any percentage applies. It is the
  single strongest argument for the annual plan §7.2 lists as undecided: at €48/yr the same fixed fee is
  0.5%, and net rises from ~€3.84×12 = €46 to about €51.
- **A premium (rewards/business) card costs 2.8% + €0.25, not 1.5%** — a mix assumption, not a constant.
- ⚠️ **Whether €5 is VAT-inclusive or exclusive is not decided anywhere.** If exclusive, a German
  customer pays €5.95 and roughly €4.58 reaches us. This single unstated choice moves net revenue ~19%.

### 7.2 Infrastructure this document never counted

| Cost | Status | Note |
|---|---|---|
| **Open-Meteo** | ⚠️ **LICENSING EXPOSURE** | The free API is **not permitted for commercial use** — verified 2026-08-12. `CLAUDE.md` records it as "free, no key", which was true while nothing was sold. Weather is on the critical path of every generate. A paid tier is required the day Pro is charged for, and CC BY 4.0 attribution is mandatory in the app regardless. |
| **Supabase egress** | **Not counted, likely dominant** | §2 measured STORAGE (330 kB/item) but never bandwidth. Every closet screen, flat-lay and diary cell serves cutouts through signed URLs, so egress scales with *engagement*, not just library size — and egress is the metered line, not gigabytes at rest. **This needs measuring before any model is trusted.** |
| **Supabase plan** | Not counted | Free tier caps DB, storage, egress and MAU; Pro is $25/mo plus usage. |
| **Vercel** | Not counted | ⚠️ Hobby is **non-commercial only**, so a paid product needs Pro at **$20/mo**. That also removes the cron restriction recorded in `plans/scoping/2026-08-11-notifications.md`. |
| **Domain** | Not counted | ~€12/yr. |
| **App store commission** | Not counted, future | If Capacitor ships (Phase 4+), Apple requires In-App Purchase for a digital subscription: **15% under the Small Business Program, otherwise 30%** — replacing Stripe's ~7%, not adding to it. Verify current terms before committing; it changes the price you must charge to net the same. |

### 7.3 The shape of the model

```
Break-even subscribers  =  fixed monthly costs
                           ─────────────────────────────────────────
                           net revenue/Pro − (cost to serve 1 Pro
                                              + free users per Pro
                                                × cost to serve 1 free)
```

Everything on the right except *fixed monthly costs* and *free users per Pro* is measurable today. The
two unmeasured inputs are **Supabase egress per active user** and the **Open-Meteo commercial tier**.

**Worked illustration — not a forecast, and not advice.** Using this document's own measured figures
(free ≈ $0.14/mo AI, Pro ≈ $0.90/mo heavy), €3.84 net, fixed costs of Vercel $20 + Supabase $25 + domain
≈ **$46/mo**, and §2's 5% conversion (so 19 free users per Pro):

```
contribution per Pro ≈ 3.84 − (0.90 + 19 × 0.14) ≈ €0.28
break-even ≈ 46 / 0.28 ≈ 164 Pro subscribers ≈ 3,300 total users
```

⚠️ **That €0.28 is razor-thin and is the real finding.** It is dominated by the *free* users each payer
carries, not by the payer. Three levers move it far more than price does: conversion rate (halve the
free-per-Pro ratio and contribution roughly doubles), free-tier AI usage (§2 already says *"if real usage
runs above ~2 generations/day for free users, lower the free allowance to 2 before raising the price"* —
that sentence is now load-bearing), and annual billing (§7.1). Egress, once measured, can only push it
down.

**Do not treat the number as a plan.** It omits the two unmeasured inputs above, assumes every card is
an EEA standard card, and assumes 5% conversion, which is an aspiration rather than an observation.

## 8. Open questions

- **Annual pricing.** €5/mo implies roughly €48/yr at the usual discount. Not decided — but §7.1 gives
  it a hard number: Stripe's €0.25 fixed fee is 5% of a monthly charge and 0.5% of an annual one, so
  annual is worth roughly €5/subscriber/year in fees alone, before any retention benefit.
- **Is €5 VAT-inclusive or exclusive?** Not decided anywhere, and it moves net revenue about 19%. §7.1.
- **The Open-Meteo commercial licence.** ⚠️ Not optional once Pro is sold. §7.2.
- **3D avatar**: inside €5, or the reason a second tier exists? Uncostable until scoped — §3.
- **Trial.** A 14-day Pro trial after the fifth wear log would land when the analytics finally have data
  to show. Not decided.
- **Regional pricing.** Euro is the design's currency; the app targets the EU and Supabase is EU-region.
  Needs a decision alongside the currency setting in Settings.
- **"See curated picks."** Affiliate partner, disclosure requirements, and whether recommendations may
  ever influence what the stylist suggests. **They must not** — the moment purchase incentives touch
  outfit ranking, the one-sentence why stops being trustworthy, and that sentence is the product.

181	|---|---|

246	⚠️ **The constraint that shapes it: `saveLocation` persists `location_timezone`, and that value comes
247	from `fetchForecast`** (`&timezone=auto`), so today location is only written as a side-effect of a
248	successful generate (`stylist.tsx:186`). Settings has no generate. `location_timezone` is load-bearing —
249	`localDateFor` and `predictDefaultOccasion` read it and a null falls back to UTC, the exact bug Decision 5
250	exists to prevent. **So Settings needs a `setLocation` action that fetches the forecast purely to resolve

## Merged (PR #31) — queue #12a, the evening wear confirmation

606 tests · `tsc` clean · `build` clean · lint at main's baseline. Live-verified in Chrome.

Replaces the twice-rejected "Auto-log worn looks" toggle. After 18:00 local, if a look was OPENED today
and nothing was logged, ask once — Yes / No.

### ⚠️ The one bug, and the plan is what caught it

**"Yes" could delete the wear it had just confirmed.** `answerWearConfirmation` called `toggleWear`, and
that is a TOGGLE — against an outfit already logged today it removes the row. **Fixed in `3c8f223`**: the
Yes path now checks for an existing log and only calls `toggleWear` when there is none.

Unreachable through the sheet (`shouldAsk` refuses once a wear exists — verified live), but a Server
Action is a public endpoint, so a double-submit or any future caller would have silently deleted real
data. It surfaced only because the plan specified *"answer Yes twice, still exactly one row"* as a
verification step, which the implementation would have failed.

### What the design encodes, and why it is not negotiable

- **Yes and No are built from ONE shared class string**, with a test asserting they are equal. Two lists
  that merely look alike are two things that can drift. No Skip / Not now / Close either: the easiest
  escape becomes the default answer, and here the default would be a lie.
- **Only looks actually OPENED are asked about.** Nothing recorded an open before this — `outfits.viewed_at`
  is the plan's one schema change. ⚠️ **Stamped from the CLIENT on mount, never in the route's render**:
  mutating during render is a side effect React may run twice, and it would fire for a prefetch the user
  never saw.
- **The backdrop records nothing**, so a mis-tap does not consume the day's only chance to log the wear.
- **`wearAskedOn` is written BEFORE the wear write.** A missed log beats a sheet that reappears until the
  user answers the way it wants.
- **`localHourFor` pins `hourCycle: "h23"`** — some locales render midnight as "24", which never compares
  below the evening threshold and would ask at 00:00.

**Local dev data was reverted**: timezone back to `Europe/Zurich`, `wearAskedOn` cleared, the test wear
log and all `viewed_at` stamps removed. ⚠️ **`profiles.tier` is still `pro`** (user request, 2026-08-10)
so Pro-gated surfaces can be exercised. Location is Rapperswil / Europe/Zurich.

truncated past 21 bottoms or shoes; and even truncating, the breadth-first walk has already varied bottom
and shoe per pass, while pinning collapses diversify's top-freshness tier. The plan's "twenty variations
of one idea" is true of the **daily** path only. Shipped anyway (user: *"if we have it in plan, then we
need it"*) because it cannot harm and becomes load-bearing at `want: 2`.

## Merged (PR #28) — queue #9b, Settings

`candidates.ts` indexed shoes at `(t + d * 2) % shoes.length`. With a single top, `t` is always 0, so the
index reduced to `2d % shoes.length` and **never left 0 whenever that length was even** — a two-shoe
closet could only ever wear the first pair, and the identical combo was emitted twice. Verified present
on `main`. A fixed stride shares a factor with every even list length; `decorrelatedStride` picks one
coprime with the count, keeping shoes off lockstep with bottoms while still visiting all of them. PR #14
measured shoe coverage on a 20-top closet, where the top index supplied the variation and hid this.

|---|---|

**`MONETISATION.md` contradicted itself.** §1 said the daily drop must never be gated; §2 counted drops
toward a limit of 3/day — with drops counted, a free user who viewed three occasions is refused the

| Style a look around a piece | **gated** | unlimited |
| New pieces added | **10 per day** (a RATE, not a closet cap) | unlimited |
| Re-opening anything already generated | free | free |

171	The reusable vocabulary, in the order the screen uses it:
172	
173	| Pattern | How it works |
174	|---|---|
175	| **Brand kicker** | Uppercase, letterspaced, muted, tiny — sits *above* the title (`HARTLEY`). Wayfinding, never content. |
176	| **Serif display title** | Libre Caslon Text, large, cream. The name of the thing (`Pale Blue Oxford`). |
177	| **Grotesk subtitle** | Hanken Grotesk, muted, `·` as the separator (`Oxford shirt · Pale blue`). |
178	| **Stat tiles** | A row of 3 rounded surfaces: serif value on top, uppercase micro-label under it (`30 / TIMES WORN`). The row is the screen's "how you actually wear it" summary. |
179	| **Labelled meter** | Uppercase kicker left, plain-language value right (`FORMALITY … Smart casual`), then 5 segments with the filled ones in rust. Never a number on its own — always the word. |
180	| **Spec table** | Hairline-divided rows, muted label left, cream value right. Multi-values joined with `·` (`Spring · Autumn · Winter`). |
181	| **Horizontal card row** | Uppercase kicker (`GOES WITH`) over a scrolling row of cutout cards with a caption under each. |
182	| **Bottom action bar** | One small secondary icon button + one full-width cream pill for the single primary action (`Style an outfit with this`). One primary action per screen. |

189	`item-data-completeness`, for cost/wear) and wear logging (queue #4 `outfit-detail-wear-logging`, for

**User decision, 2026-07-28: "we should still follow this detail page for cloth, it's the best."** When
a new screen has no design of its own — a generated concept, a Pro feature, an empty state — derive it
from this one. It is the most complete expression of the system, and the plan that builds it is queue #5
(`2026-07-24-item-detail-rebuild.md`).

The reusable vocabulary, in the order the screen uses it:

| Pattern | How it works |
|---|---|
| **Brand kicker** | Uppercase, letterspaced, muted, tiny — sits *above* the title (`HARTLEY`). Wayfinding, never content. |
| **Serif display title** | Libre Caslon Text, large, cream. The name of the thing (`Pale Blue Oxford`). |
| **Grotesk subtitle** | Hanken Grotesk, muted, `·` as the separator (`Oxford shirt · Pale blue`). |
| **Stat tiles** | A row of 3 rounded surfaces: serif value on top, uppercase micro-label under it (`30 / TIMES WORN`). The row is the screen's "how you actually wear it" summary. |
| **Labelled meter** | Uppercase kicker left, plain-language value right (`FORMALITY … Smart casual`), then 5 segments with the filled ones in rust. Never a number on its own — always the word. |
| **Spec table** | Hairline-divided rows, muted label left, cream value right. Multi-values joined with `·` (`Spring · Autumn · Winter`). |
| **Horizontal card row** | Uppercase kicker (`GOES WITH`) over a scrolling row of cutout cards with a caption under each. |
| **Bottom action bar** | One small secondary icon button + one full-width cream pill for the single primary action (`Style an outfit with this`). One primary action per screen. |

Two things this screen encodes that are easy to lose: **cutouts are the hero and everything else is
quiet around them**, and **the rust accent appears exactly once** (the meter) — the One Rust Rule in
`DESIGN.md`. A concept with two rust elements is already off-system.

Note the dependency chain this screen implies: its stat tiles need price (queue #3
`item-data-completeness`, for cost/wear) and wear logging (queue #4 `outfit-detail-wear-logging`, for
times-worn and last-worn). That is why #5 sits behind them. And `Style an outfit with this` is still an
**open decision** — see "Open decisions blocking a plan" above; it conflicts with Decision 5.

210	  if (t === undefined) return m!;
211	  if (m === undefined) return t;

214	  return material && INSULATION.has(material) ? Math.max(blended, m) : blended;

443	> re-litigated or quietly reverted. Task 1 now specifies `itemWarmth(material, texture)`; it originally
444	> specified `textureWarmth(texture)` alone.
445	
446	**Context:** `seasons-soft-preference` (PR #16) deleted the season hard filter and replaced its
447	incidental thermal protection with `HOT_MATERIALS` in `lib/generator/rules.ts` — a keyword list matched
448	against free-text `material`. That list is a stopgap. `item-data-completeness` (queue #3) constrains
449	`material` to an enum, at which point `shearling` and `puffer` stop matching entirely and `quilted`
450	becomes a texture, so the rule silently half-breaks. This plan is where warmth ends up, and Task 1
451	Step 6 is where the stopgap is finally narrowed.
452	
453	**The defect that was fixed:** this plan defined `textureWarmth(texture: string | null)` —
454	texture only. That is insufficient, and it is the mirror image of the mistake `HOT_MATERIALS` makes.
455	Trace the garments the current rule catches:
456	
457	| garment | material | texture | reads warm on texture alone? |
458	|---|---|---|---|
459	| fleece | Fleece | Fleece-back | yes |
460	| puffer | Down | Quilted | yes |
461	| shearling coat | Other | Pile | yes, by luck |
462	| **tweed jacket** | **Tweed** | Twill / Herringbone | **no** |
463	
464	Tweed's warmth lives in the cloth, not the knit structure, and `Twill`/`Herringbone` are weaves a linen
465	shirt also uses. Hence `itemWarmth(material, texture)` in Task 1: texture carries knit structure,
466	material carries fibre warmth, and the combination is what separates a chunky merino sweater from a
467	fine merino tee — the distinction that motivated all of this.
468	
469	The origin is worth keeping: the user, who knows menswear, rejected a rule that excluded **wool** above
470	25°C with *"it depends which type of wool, also his weight, weave."* Tropical, fresco and high-twist
471	wools are summer suiting, and merino is worn *for* heat because it wicks. **Fibre alone never decides
472	warmth.** Task 1's merino and tweed tests pin both halves of that.
473	
474	**Keep a narrow hard exclusion for insulation.** A soft term demotes but does not prevent, and
475	`diversify` fills the shortlist to 20, so a down puffer can still reach the screen at 32°C on a thin
476	closet. There is a real difference between *slightly off-season* — which this project deliberately
477	accepts ("better a slightly-off outfit than none") — and *physically wrong*. Keep down / fleece /
478	shearling excluded above roughly 28°C, because no weave rescues them. This is safe now in a way it was
479	not before: `eligibleByCategory`'s relief rule guarantees a weather exclusion can narrow a required
480	slot but never empty it.
481	
482	**Net result:** narrow `HOT_MATERIALS` to `["fleece", "down", "shearling"]` when this ships — Task 1
483	Step 6 — not when queue #3 ships. Between #3 and here it is degraded but not useless: `fleece`, `down`
484	and `tweed` still match the constrained vocabulary, while `shearling`, `puffer` and `quilted` stop.
485	
486	**Limit worth stating:** even `warmth(material, texture)` is not a weight model. `texture` captures knit
487	structure and surface finish, not gsm, so a tropical-weight wool trouser and a flannel one can both be
488	`Flat` and score identically. Better than a keyword list by a wide margin; not the last word.

# Executing Plans

## Overview

Load plan, review critically, execute all tasks, report when complete.

**Announce at start:** "I'm using the executing-plans skill to implement this plan."

**Note:** Tell your human partner that Superpowers works much better with access to subagents (Claude Code, Codex CLI, Codex App, Copilot CLI, and Gemini CLI all qualify; see the per-platform tool refs in `../using-superpowers/references/`). If subagents are available, use superpowers:subagent-driven-development instead of this skill.

## The Process

### Step 1: Load and Review Plan
1. Ensure an isolated workspace: use superpowers:using-git-worktrees to create one or verify the existing one
2. Read plan file
3. Review critically - identify any questions or concerns about the plan
4. If concerns: Raise them with your human partner before starting
5. If no concerns: Create todos for the plan items and proceed

### Step 2: Execute Tasks

For each task:
1. Mark as in_progress
2. Follow each step exactly (plan has bite-sized steps)
3. Run verifications as specified
4. Mark as completed

### Step 3: Complete Development

After all tasks complete and verified:
- Announce: "I'm using the finishing-a-development-branch skill to complete this work."
- **REQUIRED SUB-SKILL:** Use superpowers:finishing-a-development-branch
- Follow that skill to verify tests, present options, execute choice

## When to Stop and Ask for Help

**STOP executing immediately when:**
- Hit a blocker (missing dependency, test fails, instruction unclear)
- Plan has critical gaps preventing starting
- You don't understand an instruction
- Verification fails repeatedly

**Ask for clarification rather than guessing.**

## When to Revisit Earlier Steps

**Return to Review (Step 1) when:**
- Partner updates the plan based on your feedback
- Fundamental approach needs rethinking

**Don't force through blockers** - stop and ask.

## Remember
- Review plan critically first
- Follow plan steps exactly
- Don't skip verifications
- Reference skills when plan says to
- Stop when blocked, don't guess
- Never start implementation on main/master branch without explicit user consent

content.text:
Right — here's the picture before I write anything.

## What plan #13 is

The tagger has always written two fields the generator never reads: **`pattern`** and **`texture`**. So today:

- A **cable-knit sweater and a flat oxford** are interchangeable to the ranker in February. Nothing knows one is warm.
- Nothing stops a **striped shirt being paired with a checked trouser**.

The plan adds both as **soft scoring terms** — the model this codebase has landed on three times now (outerwear, colour lean, season). Neither may ever eliminate a candidate; a closet where every top is patterned must still produce outfits.

Three pieces of work:

1. **`lib/generator/texture.ts`** — `itemWarmth(material, texture)` → 0..1, and `warmthFit(items, tempC)`. Warmth reads **both** dimensions on purpose. Texture alone misses tweed (its warmth is in the cloth, and `Twill`/`Herringbone` are weaves a linen shirt also uses); material alone misses the merino case (a chunky merino knit and a fine merino tee share a fibre and are a season apart). This is your own correction from the seasons work, encoded.
2. **Pattern clash + warmth in `scoreCombo`** — one loud piece is a statement, two are an argument.
3. **This is where `HOT_MATERIALS` finally dies.** That keyword list in `rules.ts` was the stopgap left behind when the season hard-filter was deleted. It narrows to `fleece / down / shearling` — genuine insulation that no weave rescues — and `tweed`, `quilted`, `puffer` come out (tweed moves to scoring; the other two never matched the constrained vocabulary anyway).

## What I found checking the plan against the actual code and your closet

Your local closet is 21 items, all tagged. Two things matter:

**Texture varies usefully** — 4 cable-knit tops against flat/fine-knit shirts and two linen oxfords. So the warmth signal is genuinely verifiable live: a cold day should favour the cable knits, a hot day the linen.

**Every single item is `solid`.** The pattern term will be completely inert on this closet — I can unit-test it but I cannot prove it fires in a real generate.

## My questions

**1. The weight budget — the plan contradicts itself, and this one's yours to call.**

Score today is `base` (colour harmony + formality coherence + Style DNA) with two preferences carved out of it: colour lean takes 0.3 when you use Refine, season takes 0.2. Both active → base keeps exactly half. The plan says warmth takes another 0.15 *and* says "base must keep at least half when every preference is active." Those can't both be true — you'd land at 0.35.

In practice all three are only ever active when you've used Refine (season is always on, lean only on request). So:

- **Cap the total preference share at 0.5 and scale** — the invariant holds literally, existing behaviour is byte-identical (today's max is already exactly 0.5), and any future preference term is protected too. Costs: when you Refine, warmth's real weight is ~0.115 rather than 0.15.
- **Or just let base drop to 0.35** when you Refine — simpler, and arguably honest: if you asked for olive *and* it's 2°C, maybe the raw aesthetic score *should* have less say.

I lean to the cap, because it's the invariant the plan itself wrote down and it's the future-proof shape. But it's a "what the stylist prioritises" call, so I'd rather you picked.

**2. Do you want me to temporarily tag one item as `striped` and another as `check` to prove the pattern term actually moves a live generate — then revert it?** Same pattern as the Manila/rain-guard verification. Otherwise pattern ships unit-tested only, and I'll say exactly that rather than claim it's verified.

**3. One heads-up, not a question:** narrowing `HOT_MATERIALS` means a **tweed** jacket is no longer banned above 25°C — merely scored down. That's the plan's deliberate intent (fibre alone never decides warmth was your point), and outerwear isn't required above 15°C anyway, so the exposure is small. Say if you'd rather keep tweed hard-excluded.

**One call I'm making myself** unless you object: the plan's material table omits `Leather`, `Suede` and `Faux leather`, which is all three of your shoes. They'd fall through to texture-only. I'll add them at sensible values (suede reads warmer than smooth leather — nap traps air, and it's a cold-season shoe).

Good question, and worth being precise about it: **weather is one of three pillars, not the only one.** `CLAUDE.md`'s own one-liner is *"matched to occasion, weather, and your aesthetic."* That's exactly why warmth is a scored signal rather than a filter — an app that only optimises for temperature dresses you correctly and looks like nothing. But you're right that weather is where we're currently weakest: the generator reads a *month* (season tags) rather than the actual temperature and the actual cloth. That's what this plan fixes, so I'll build it to be genuinely good rather than minimally to spec.

Four decisions, then I build:

1. **Climate becomes one term, not two competing ones.** Season and warmth answer the same question, so instead of adding a third preference that squeezes the budget, they merge: `climate = 0.7 × warmthFit + 0.3 × seasonFit`, weighted **0.28** (up from season's 0.2). Real temperature × real fabric leads; the month tag grounds it. No scaling hack, weather gets a *stronger* voice than today, and future weather work (wind, humidity) goes inside that term instead of fighting for weight.
2. **Warmth is weighted by category.** Averaging a gold watch and a pair of shoes into your warmth score drags every outfit toward neutral exactly when the signal should be loudest. Outerwear and tops count most, shoes little, accessories almost nothing.
3. **The plan's own test #10 fails against the plan's own implementation** — I checked the arithmetic. It wants the signal to stop dominating in mild weather; a linear fit doesn't do that once material blending is added (the gap is identical at 18° and 0°). I'll add the confidence damping the plan's prose describes so the term genuinely goes quiet around 12°C.
4. Leather/suede added to the warmth table; pattern verified live by temporarily tagging two items, then reverted.

*
 * This is the measured replacement for the season tag's incidental thermal
 * protection: season used to be a hard filter, so a sweater tagged
 * {Autumn,Winter} could never reach a July outfit. Season is now a preference
 * (see ./season.ts), so the guard moved to the temperature we already fetch.
 *
 * The list is deliberately SHORT, and notably does not contain wool.
 * Whether a wool garment suits 30°C is decided by its weight and weave, not its
 * fibre: tropical, fresco and high-twist wools are summer suiting, and merino is
 * used *for* heat because it wicks and breathes. `items.material` is a bare
 * fibre name today, so a "wool" rule cannot tell a summer-weight trouser from a
 * melton coat — it would exclude exactly the smart-casual work wear this app is
 * built around. Everything left here is insulation or a coarse heavy weave,
 * where no construction makes it summer-appropriate.
 *
 * Wool, merino and cashmere are not unprotected: an off-season piece still takes
 * the `seasonFit` penalty in scoring, so it ranks below linen in July. Demoted
 * on evidence rather than eliminated on a guess — the same argument this module
 * makes about season itself.
 *
 * The real fix is data, not a longer list. `item-data-completeness` (queue #3)
 * adds an `items.texture` column — Flat / Fine knit / Chunky knit / Brushed /
 * Fleece-back — and constrains `material` to a vocabulary that separates "Wool"
 * from "Merino wool". `item-signals-in-generator` (queue #12) then feeds
 * material × texture into SCORING. Warmth belongs there, as a weighted signal,
 * not here as a veto.
 */
const HOT_MATERIALS = ["fleece", "shearling", "down", "quilted", "puffer", "tweed"];

/** Strictly above 25: 24° is pleasant, 26° is hot. */
const HOT_C = 25;

_Last updated: 2026-08-13 (**IN FLIGHT: `feat/item-signals`, 3 commits, NOT pushed, no PR opened** —
queue #13. All gates green, live-verified. `main` = `2aeb68e`. **#8 was absorbed into #7; do not execute
it.**) Read this first when resuming._

## In flight — queue #13, `feat/item-signals`

640 tests · `tsc` clean · `build` clean · lint identical to main's baseline (13 problems, all
pre-existing). Live-verified in the iPhone 17 Pro simulator.

**Three deliberate divergences from the plan, all decided with the user 2026-08-13 ("make what would be
the best to implement it and for future… it should perfectly show clothes that would fit on specific
weather").**

1. **Season and warmth are ONE `climate` term, not two competing preferences.** The plan added warmth
   at 0.15 *and* asserted "base keeps at least half when every preference is active" — those cannot
   both hold (0.3 lean + 0.2 season + 0.15 warmth leaves base 0.35). Merged instead:
   `climate = 0.7·warmthFit + 0.3·seasonFit` at `CLIMATE_WEIGHT = 0.28`. Weather gets a *stronger*
   voice than before, the budget is bounded by construction, and future weather work (wind, humidity)
   belongs inside the term rather than beside it. ⚠️ `SEASON_WEIGHT` no longer exists.
2. **`warmthFit` weights by category** (outerwear 1.5 / tops 1.2 / bottoms 1 / shoes 0.6 / accessories
   0.2 / fragrance 0). A flat average let a steel watch and a pair of shoes drag every combo toward
   neutral exactly when the signal should be loudest. Matched by *prefix on the lowercased category*, so
   DB TitleCase (`Tops`) and the singular test fixtures (`top`) both land.
3. **⚠️ The plan's own test #10 FAILED against the plan's own implementation.** "The warmth signal
   discriminates less in mild weather than in the cold" cannot pass with a bare `1 - |want - have|`:
   once `want` sits outside the two warmth values the gap between them is CONSTANT, so 18° and 0°
   discriminate identically. The plan's inline arithmetic assumed texture-only warmth (0.9 vs 0.25) and
   silently broke once material blending was added. Fixed with a `confidence = |want - 0.5| · 2` factor
   that fades the whole term to neutral at 12.5°, which is what the plan's prose always described.
   **Do not "simplify" that factor away — the test is the reason it exists.**

**Also diverged, smaller:** `Leather`/`Suede`/`Faux leather` added to `MATERIAL_WARMTH` (the plan omitted
them, and they are all three pairs of shoes in the dev closet); `tempC` threaded into
`style-actions.ts` too, not just `app/generate/actions.ts` — the plan names only the daily path, but a
look built around a chosen piece still has to be wearable today.

### `HOT_MATERIALS` is finally dead as a warmth rule

Narrowed to `["fleece", "shearling", "down"]`. ⚠️ **`tweed` is no longer hard-excluded above 25°** — its
warmth moved to `MATERIAL_WARMTH`, so it is scored down rather than banned, exactly as wool already was.
`quilted` and `puffer` were removed as **dead**: `Quilted` is a TEXTURE and `puffer` is in no vocabulary,
so neither had matched anything since `material` became an enum.

### Measured on the real 21-item closet (deterministic, no AI spend)

| tempC | top 3 of the shortlist |
|---|---|
| 0 / 8 / 12 | Cable knit · Cable knit · Flat |
| 18 / 25 / 32 | Linen · Linen · Fine knit |

The crossover sits between 12° and 18°, and it flips **against a constant `season: "Summer"`** in the
probe — so warmth, not the tag, is doing it. **Pattern clash:** the dev closet is 100% `solid`, so it was
measured by re-tagging two garments *in memory* (no DB write, nothing to revert) — the two-loud combo
falls **#54 → #65 of 66** while the one-loud combo holds #35 at an identical score.

⚠️ **Honest limit of the live run:** at 23°C the generator returned Linen for look 01 but cable knits for
02 and 03. That is not a warmth failure — with only ~7 distinct tops, `diversify` fills its 20 shortlist
slots with nearly the whole closet, so the AI re-ranker sees the knits regardless and warmth only
reorders. On a larger closet the shortlist would actually exclude them.

### Local dev data — what this session changed

- **Today's `work` daily drop was deleted and regenerated** (one real Haiku call, 2.8s). No wear log
  pointed at those rows. The styled looks and the other three occasions were untouched.
- **A dev server the user had running on :3000 (PID 45318) was stopped and restarted** so the new code
  was certainly what got served.
- ⚠️ **A `wear_logs` row appeared mid-session that this session did not intend**: `622baacc…` against
  styled outfit `01a38225…`, written 22:20 local by `answerWearConfirmation(…, true)`. The evening sheet
  was on screen when the Simulator was brought to the front; synthetic taps do not work on this machine
  (System Events `-25204`), so it was almost certainly a real tap by the user. **Left in place
  deliberately — deleting a possibly-genuine answer is worse than leaving one row.** Confirm and delete
  if it was not intentional.

content.text:
Cap **and** floor. Here's the deciding argument, which isn't the one I gave you before.

A cap on its own is lopsided in the wrong direction. If Summer-tagged pieces get pulled toward neutral but Winter-tagged pieces never get pushed up, then on a cold day everything bunches together — the signal loses resolution *specifically in winter*, which is exactly where wearing the wrong thing actually costs you something. In August a mistake is uncomfortable; in February it's a bad day. Symmetric is better.

But the floor should be gentler than the cap, because the two tags aren't equally meaningful. "I wear this in summer" is nearly always a statement about heat. "I only wear this in winter" is sometimes about style — a dark colour, a heavy look — not temperature.

So, three changes:

- **`Cable knit` drops 0.8 → 0.7.** The cable is a *stitch pattern*, not a weight. This is the honest fix independent of tags.
- **Summer in the tags caps warmth at 0.55** — you've said it works in heat, so no photo-derived reading may call it insulation. Genuine insulation (fleece/down/shearling) is exempt; that's the one case where physics outranks the tag, and it's already hard-excluded above 25° anyway.
- **Winter without Summer floors it at 0.65** — the black crew neck should read warm, not the same as your summer polos.

them, and they are all three pairs of shoes in the dev closet); `tempC` threaded into

### ⚠️ 4. The wearer's season tags CONSTRAIN warmth (user correction, 2026-08-13)

> *"I can't say that cable knit is only for cold weather, I have 2 pieces of wardrobe that are cable
> knit and they are good for summer in 18-27."*

**He was right, and his closet already said so** — two of his four cable-knit pieces carry a Summer tag.
`Cable knit: 0.8` was **the same conflation `HOT_MATERIALS` made with "wool", one level down**: a cable
is a STITCH PATTERN, not a weight, so a cotton cable polo and an aran sweater share the value and are
seasons apart. Lowered to **0.7** on its own merits.

The structural half matters more. `material` and `texture` are **inferred by Haiku from a photograph**
that cannot see yarn weight or gsm; `seasons` is **the field the user edits and confirms**. The first
draft weighted the guess at 0.7 and the confirmed answer at 0.3, so on exactly the garments where they
disagree, the guess won. Now the tag clamps warmth per garment inside `itemWarmth`:

- **Summer present → warmth capped at `SUMMER_CAP` 0.55.**
- **Winter present and Summer absent → floored at `WINTER_FLOOR` 0.65.** Asymmetric deliberately:
  "I wear this in summer" is nearly always thermal, "only in winter" is sometimes about style.
- ⚠️ **Two exemptions, and they are the point of the design** — `INSULATION` (fleece/down/shearling) is
  exempt from the CAP, `COOLING` (linen) from the FLOOR. These are the two ends where physics outranks
  the wearer. **The linen exemption was found by a failing test, not by inspection:** without it a linen
  shirt tagged Winter is lifted to 0.65 and competes with knitwear in February.
- ⚠️ **Clamp inside `itemWarmth`, NOT a heavier `seasonFit` weight.** A heavier weight lets the tag
  out-shout warmth on *every* piece; the clamp corrects only the garments the photo got wrong.

**A score test had to be rewritten, not the implementation.** "Real cloth at a real temperature outweighs
the month tag" encoded the belief this correction overturns. Replaced by two tests that state the new
hierarchy: where the tags AGREE the fabric decides; where the tag SPEAKS it outranks the photo.

**Measured on the real closet** (`itemWarmth` / `warmthFit` per garment):

| cable-knit piece | Summer tag | fit @22° | fit @2° |
|---|---|---|---|
| Cable knit polo (navy) · Polo shirt (cream) | yes | **0.553** | 0.609 |
| Cable knit polo (brown) · crew neck (black) | no | 0.477 | **0.693** |

And in the shortlist at `season: "Winter"`, 0°C now leads with the two NON-Summer cable knits; by 12°C
the Summer-tagged pair has taken the top two places.

gh pr create --title "feat: texture, pattern and the wearer's season tags influence ranking" --body "$(cat <<'EOF'
The tagger has always written `pattern`, and `texture` arrived with the
item-data work. The generator read neither, so a chunky knit and a fine knit
were interchangeable in February, and nothing stopped a striped shirt being
paired with a checked trouser.

Both enter as soft preferences — the model this codebase has landed on three
times now (outerwear, colour lean, season). Neither can eliminate a candidate:
a closet where every top is patterned still produces outfits, and an untagged
texture counts as neutral rather than as a penalty.

## Climate is one term, not two

Season and warmth answer the same question with different evidence, so they
share a weight rather than competing for the score: `climate = 0.7·warmthFit +
0.3·seasonFit` at `CLIMATE_WEIGHT` 0.28, up from season's 0.2. Adding warmth as
a third independent preference would have squeezed colour, formality and DNA
below half the score whenever a Refine lean was also active. Future weather work
belongs inside this term, not beside it.

Warmth is weighted by category (outerwear 1.5 / tops 1.2 / bottoms 1 / shoes 0.6
/ accessories 0.2). A flat average let a steel watch and a pair of shoes drag
every combo toward neutral exactly when the signal should be loudest.

## What's next

It's a **simulation**: "if you owned a hypothetical item X, how many new combos would exist?" Nobody has designed what X is, how it's proposed, or how the count is computed without running the generator dozens of times. The plan also predates the entitlements seam, so the Pro gate has to be added — with the caveat that the item-detail wear tiles (times worn, cost-per-wear, last worn) **stay free**, which you already confirmed. A fact about the piece in your hand is free; the screen that analyses your whole wardrobe is Pro.

**Unblocked and a natural follow-on: #15's whole-generator pass.** We've just rewritten scoring for the fourth time. That plan's coverage and regenerate halves are done and measured; what remains is the end-to-end review of the pipeline as it now stands. Doing it while this work is fresh is cheaper than doing it cold in a month.

Then #14 (route/URL audit) and #16 (full design audit), both of which deliberately run last.

**Two things outside the queue that I'd rather you saw now than at launch:**

- **Open-Meteo's free API is not licensed for commercial use** — and after this PR, weather is more central to the product than it has ever been. It's on the critical path of every single generation. This needs resolving before Pro is sold, not after.
- **Packing mode is advertised in the upgrade sheet and does not exist.** That was a deliberate call while nothing can be bought, but it has to be built or removed from the copy before there's a checkout.

My recommendation: merge #32, then decide the wear-stats gap-analysis question — because if you'd rather not design that now, #15 is ready to go instead.

Good catch — it partly works, and the measurement says exactly how much:

| temperature | best sweater combo, of 66 | shortlist slot the model sees |
|---|---|---|
| 20° | #13 | **#13 of 20** |
| 27° | #22 | **#13 of 20** |
| 34° | #22 | **#13 of 20** |

So the warmth term **is** demoting it — #13 → #22 as the day heats up. But it reaches the model anyway at every temperature, and Haiku then picked it and wrote *"add warmth appropriate for the mild weather."*

Two separate defects, and the first is the bigger one.

## 1. We dress you for *this minute*, not for today

`mapForecast` returns `raw.current.temperature_2m`. Your drop was generated when it was 20°. The real day is **20.5° at 07:00 → 34.8° at 17:00**. Even a perfect warmth signal is optimising the wrong number — you get dressed once and live in that outfit through the peak.

Open-Meteo already returns `daily.temperature_2m_max`; we simply never ask for it. The hourly strip we do fetch only looks **4 hours ahead**, which at 07:45 stops well before the heat.

## 2. On a 21-item closet, a soft signal can't keep a sweater out

66 combos, and `diversify` fills 20 shortlist slots — **30% of everything reaches the model**. Dropping from #13 to #22 doesn't remove it, it just reshuffles which 20 get through. This is precisely the hole the plan itself warned about: *"a soft term demotes, and `diversify` still fills 20 slots."* We kept a hard exclusion only for fleece/down/shearling — and a cotton cable-knit sweater isn't insulation by material, so nothing stopped it.

The fix I'd write: above ~28°, hard-exclude anything whose computed `itemWarmth` is ≥ 0.6, using the existing relief rule so it can still never empty a required slot. That's a threshold on the *new* number rather than another keyword list — and because that number now respects your season tags, it separates your closet correctly: the black crew neck (0.65) and the brown polo (0.65) are out at 34°, while your two Summer-tagged cable knits (0.55) stay in.

## The question I need you to answer

**Which temperature should the day's looks be built for?** There's no obviously right answer:

- **Today's high** — you're never too hot, but at 07:00 in 20° you're underdressed.
- **The daytime mean** (roughly 28° today) — splits the difference, wrong at both ends.
- **The high, plus honest layering advice** — dress for the peak and let the "Later" line say *"chilly until 10 — take a layer."* That strip already exists and only looks 4 hours out; extending it to the full day is the natural companion.

I lean to the third: for a hot day, being over-dressed at breakfast is a smaller failure than being in a cable knit at 35° all afternoon, and the advice line is already the product's way of handling exactly this.

Both fixes would ride along on PR #32 rather than becoming a standalone bug PR, per the convention. Which temperature do you want?

### ⚠️ 5. The look is built for the DAY, not for the minute it was generated (user report, 2026-08-14)

> *"It shows me a sweater which has filter for autumn and winter today, yes right now 22, but it will
> be 34 celsium, so does our new updated not work?"*

**Two defects, and the first is the bigger one.**

**`mapForecast` returned `raw.current.temperature_2m` and every thermal rule read it.** The drop is
generated ONCE and worn all day, so it optimised for the minute the app happened to be opened — 20°C at
07:45, on a day that reached 34.8°C. Open-Meteo already returns `daily.temperature_2m_max`; we simply
never asked for it.

**⚠️ The decision (user, option 3 of 3): the look is built for the day's HIGH, and the cold end is
handled by ADVICE, not by the outfit.** `planningTemp(w) = w.highC ?? w.tempC` in `rules.ts` is the
single definition. Consequences, all deliberate:

- **`needsOuterwear` follows the high too.** Otherwise a 9°-morning / 22°-afternoon day puts a coat in
  every flat-lay you see at 3pm. The layer is something the advice tells you to carry.
- **Rain still reads the current hour** — wet pavement is about now; heat is about the afternoon.
- **`laterAdvice` gained a rise branch**, and it is load-bearing rather than decorative: *"Up to 35°
  this afternoon — you're dressed for it."* Without it a deliberately light look at 20°C reads as the
  stylist being wrong. Priority is rain → rise → evening drop → reassurance.
- **`highC`/`lowC` are OPTIONAL on `Weather` and on the `Raw` response**, falling back to `tempC`, so
  every existing fixture and any cached pre-change response behaves exactly as before.
- ⚠️ **The range is clamped so it can never contradict the number on screen** (`max(now, high)` /
  `min(now, low)`). A stale daily block against a fresh `current` would otherwise report a high BELOW
  what the user is reading. A test pins it — and it caught a wrong test fixture of mine first.

**Defect 2: a soft signal cannot keep a sweater out of a 34° day on a small closet.** Measured: the
warmth term DID demote it, #13 → #22 of 66 combos — but `diversify` fills 20 shortlist slots, so **30%
of everything reaches the model** and a demotion changes nothing. It then picked it and wrote *"adds
warmth appropriate for the mild weather."* This is exactly the hole the plan named: *"a soft term
demotes, and diversify still fills 20 slots."*

**Fix: above `SWELTERING_C` 28°, `itemWarmth >= 0.6` becomes a hard bar** (`weatherRules().maxWarmth`,
applied in `isEligible`). ⚠️ **It reads `itemWarmth`, NOT a material list** — that is the whole point:
the black crew neck and the navy polo are BOTH `Cotton`/`Cable knit`, and only the wearer's season tags
separate them (0.65 vs 0.55). ⚠️ **`WeatherBars` groups the material list and the warmth bar into one
object so the relief rule drops ALL of them at once** — splitting them would let the new bar survive
relief and empty a slot, the bug class this project has now fixed four times. A test pins that a closet
of nothing but heavy knitwear still produces combos at 34°.

**Verified live against the real 34.8°C forecast:** looks are Linen oxford / **Summer-tagged cable knit
polo** / Viscose polo. The Autumn/Winter crew neck is gone; the user's summer cable knit is not. The
advice strip renders *"Up to 35° this afternoon — you're dressed for it."*

**PR #32 merged.** `main` is now `2c8482a`, 668 tests green, branch deleted, plan filed in `done/`, README and `docs/STATE.md` updated.

## What queue #13 turned into

It started as "put two unused columns into scoring" and ended up rebuilding how the app thinks about weather — mostly because you pushed back twice, and both times you were right:

- **The cable-knit correction** — a stitch pattern isn't a weight, and your season tags now constrain warmth rather than argue with it.
- **The 34° sweater** — we were dressing you for the minute you opened the app instead of for the day.

Neither was in the plan. The plan's own test #10 also turned out to fail against the plan's own implementation, which is worth remembering next time a plan looks finished on paper.

## What's next

**Queue #10 `wear-stats` is nominally next but blocked on your decision** — the *"unlocks 14 new outfits"* line is a simulation, not a query, and nobody has designed what it simulates. It also needs the Pro gate retrofitted, with the item-detail wear tiles staying free.

**So the next executable work is #15's whole-generator pass.** Good timing: we've just changed scoring, eligibility and the weather input, and that plan exists to review the pipeline end to end. Doing it now while it's fresh beats doing it cold.

Then #14 (routes/URLs) and #16 (full design audit), both deliberately last.

**Two things still outside the queue that I'd rather raise now than at launch:**

- **Open-Meteo's free tier isn't licensed for commercial use** — and after today it's more central than ever. It's on the critical path of every generation.
- **Packing mode is advertised in the upgrade sheet and doesn't exist.** Fine while nothing can be bought; not fine once there's a checkout.

Also still sitting there: **13 stale branches** (2 local, 11 remote), all verified fully merged. Deleting them loses nothing — say the word and I'll clear them.

My suggestion: **#15's generator pass**, unless you'd rather settle the wear-stats question first.

content.text:
Ran three day shapes through the shipped code. **The clothes are right in all three. The advice is wrong in two** — and it's a defect I introduced yesterday.

## What it picks

| day | planning temp | outerwear | looks |
|---|---|---|---|
| Deep winter (−2° now, 3° high) | 3° | **yes, in every look** | Cable knit polo + wool trousers + jacket · cable knit crew + trousers + jacket |
| Cold evening (8° now, 1° low) | 9° | yes | same, coat included |
| Spring swing (6° now, 18° high) | 18° | **no** | Linen oxford + trousers, no coat |

That's all correct. In winter the season floor lifts your Autumn/Winter knits, the climate term wants warmth (`want` = 0.88), and `needsOuterwear` puts the jacket in every combo. The spring day is built for the 18° afternoon, exactly as you chose.

## The bug

**Winter:** *"Up to 3° this afternoon — you're dressed for it."*

The rise branch fires on any ≥5° climb, and −2 → 3 qualifies. So on a freezing day it prints a sentence written for heat, **and it suppresses the message that actually matters** (the evening drop). Nonsense copy in the exact season where advice matters most.

**Spring:** *"Up to 18° this afternoon — you're dressed for it."*

The clothes are right — but at 6° in the morning, in a linen shirt with no coat, you are emphatically *not* dressed for it. This is the **layering half of option 3 that I didn't build**. You chose "dress for the peak *plus* honest layering advice"; I shipped the explaining half and left out the layer instruction. That's on me.

## The fix

The rise branch needs two conditions it doesn't have:

- **Only fire when the day's high is genuinely warm** (~20°+), so it stops hijacking winter.
- **When it's currently cold enough to feel** (below ~15°), the clause becomes a *layer instruction* instead of reassurance — *"Cool until midday — take a layer."*

Winter then falls through to the evening-drop check, which already works: *"Down to 2° tonight — carry a jacket."*

**One copy call I'd rather you made.** A steady cold day — 3° high, no big drop — currently lands on the fallback: *"Dry through the evening — no extra layer."* True (the coat is already in the look), but flat on a freezing day. Options:

- Leave it — it's accurate and the coat is visibly in the flat-lay.
- Give cold days their own line, e.g. *"Cold all day — the coat earns its place."*

I lean to giving it its own line: the advice strip is the one place the app talks to you about the weather, and "no extra layer" at 3° reads like it hasn't noticed.

Want me to fix this on a branch? It's small — `laterAdvice` plus tests — and it rides on its own PR now that #32 is merged.

Today's numbers, so this is concrete rather than theoretical:

```
now      33.1°
day max  34.8°   ← what every look is built for
evening  19:00=34.3  20:00=32.4  21:00=28.7  22:00=27.1
```

**Limit 1 — the high is the whole calendar day's, including hours already gone.** If you first open the app at 20:00, it still plans for the 17:00 peak that's already behind you. Harmless today (34.8 vs 32.4). On an October day that hits 18° at 15:00 and falls to 7° by evening, it would send you out under-dressed — the exact mirror of the bug we just fixed.

**Limit 2 — every occasion gets the same number.** The Evening drop you generated at 14:22 was built for 34.8°, not for the evening. Today that's nearly free, because 19:00 is still 34.3°. But in autumn your Evening look would be built for the afternoon.

Both are one root cause: **one temperature for every occasion, at every hour of the day.** The honest version is the peak of the hours *still ahead that the occasion covers* — Work and Everyday look at the rest of the working day, Evening looks at 18:00–23:00. We already fetch 24 hours of forecast; `mapForecast` just throws all but four cells away for the "Later" strip, so the data is sitting there.

That's maybe an hour's work and it's the same class of correctness as what we just shipped. Your call on sequencing:

- **Do it after #15**, since the generator pass may surface related things and you'd batch them.

## Merged (PRs #33, #34) — the weather follow-ups to #32

Both came out of the user driving the real app, not from review. **#32 made the drop plan for the day's
high; these two made that actually correct.**

### PR #33 — the advice strip must match the look beside it

⚠️ **#32 shipped the half that EXPLAINS a light outfit and left out the half that tells you what to do
about the cold start** — the user had chosen "dress for the peak **plus** honest layering advice" and
only got the first half. Found by running real day shapes through the pipeline, not by reading code.

- **A −2°C day read *"Up to 3° this afternoon — you're dressed for it."*** The rise branch fired on any
  5° climb, so winter got copy written for heat **and** the evening-drop message was suppressed.
- **A 6°→18° spring morning said *"you're dressed for it"*** while the look was a linen shirt with no
  coat. At 6° you are not.

**Two rules now hold across every branch:** never tell the user to carry something the look already
includes, and never reassure them about a day they are not yet dressed for. ⚠️ **`OUTERWEAR_C` is
exported from `rules.ts` and IMPORTED by `advice.ts`** — two copies of 15 would drift, and the drift
would be invisible: the sentence would simply start disagreeing with the flat-lay beside it.

### PR #34 — plan each look for the window it will be worn in

Two limits remained, both from using ONE number (today's calendar max) for every occasion at every hour.

- **The calendar max runs midnight to midnight**, so opening at 20:00 planned against a 17:00 peak
  already lived through — the mirror of #32's bug. `mapForecast` now returns **`restOfDay`** and the
  high/low derive from it; the daily block is only the fallback. ⚠️ **`restOfDay` is restricted to the
  current local DATE**: `forecast_hours=24` runs past midnight, so an evening window matched on
  hour-of-day alone would plan against *tomorrow's* 19:00.
- **Every occasion shared that number**, so an Evening look chosen at 14:00 was built for the afternoon.
  `lib/weather/planning.ts` gives each occasion a window (work `[0,19)`, evening `[18,24)`, everyday /
  weekend `[0,22)`) and takes the warmest hour still ahead inside it. An occasion whose window has
  passed falls back to the hours that remain.

**Measured — and note why it stayed invisible:**

| scenario | Everyday | Evening |
|---|---|---|
| A 35° August day, asked at 14:00 | 35° | 34° |
| An October day, asked at 14:00 | 18° | **13°** |
| The same October day, asked at 20:00 | **8°** | 8° (was 18°) |

**In high summer the evening is as hot as the peak, so the bug costs nothing.** October is where it
sends someone out in a shirt at 7°.

⚠️ **Two of the tests written in #32 had to be REWRITTEN, not the code** — they encoded the
calendar-day model this supersedes. Same pattern as the score test in #32. When a plan's test fails
after a deliberate model change, check which one is out of date before "fixing" the implementation.

## Status — partially done, 2026-07-24

**Branch `fix/generator-coverage`, 5 commits, not yet merged.** Tasks 1-3 below were executed early at
the user's request. 213 tests / tsc / build all green. **Live verification confirmed the coverage fix
works** ("it works") — but surfaced a new symptom, recorded in "Still open" below.

### Fixed — four defects, all measured before fixing

| # | Where | Defect |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | `candidates.ts` | Top-major nested loop + `slice(0, CAP)`. Only the first top ever reached ranking. |
| 2 | `candidates.ts` | `outer[0]` / `accessories[0]` pinned to index 0 — one coat, forever. |
| 3 | `rerank.ts` | Prompt said "pick the best 3" with no requirement they differ; schema never checked the three `combo_index` values were distinct. |
| 4 | `actions.ts` | `top[p.combo_index]?.items ?? top[0].items` — an out-of-range index silently became a **copy of the first look**. |

Measured coverage, 20-per-category closet (`lib/generator/__tests__/coverage.test.ts`):

```
              before → after
tops              1  →  20  of 20
bottoms           5  →  20  of 20
shoes            20  →  20  of 20
coats             1  →   3  of 3
accessories       1  →   3  of 3
```

Also added `lib/generator/diversity.ts`: the shortlist is diversified **before** the re-ranker sees it,
so no two of the 20 candidates share a top or a bottom and whichever three the model picks are distinct
by construction. It backfills only to a floor of 3 — padding a 20-slot shortlist on a 10-top/6-bottom
closet would have handed the model 14 repeats, reintroducing the bug one layer down.

**Suspect 3 from the original analysis (a diversity pass over the final three) was killed by
measurement** and replaced by the shortlist diversifier above — the right place was the *input* to the
re-ranker, not its output.

### Still open

- **Regenerate does not work properly.** Reported by the user 2026-07-24 after live-testing the fixes:
  *"it works, but not at all, right now regenerator doesn't work properly."* **Not yet root-caused — no
  measurement taken.** See the dedicated section below.
- **The whole-generator pass** the user asked for once the other plans have shipped.
- **A second consumer of the pipeline now exists** (added 2026-07-31, PR #22):
  `app/closet/[itemId]/style-actions.ts` runs `buildCandidates → rankTopN` with an item pinned. It does
  **not** call `diversify` — it takes `pinned.slice(0, 20)`. The whole-generator pass should treat the
  shortlist rule as pipeline-wide rather than a property of `app/generate/actions.ts`. The fix itself is
  Task 1 of `todo/2026-07-31-styled-look-depth.md`; do not do it twice.
- Live verification of the coverage fix on a real closet was partial; no screenshots were taken.

gets the planning temperature, plus the current one when the day still has to
climb, and is told explicitly which of the two the outfit is for.
