Done. **Queues #13 and #15 are both complete** — five PRs merged, `main` = `fb285db`, 693 tests green, tree clean.

## The generator pass found one defect wearing three disguises

The pipeline kept reading **the current hour** for a look that is worn all day. You caught the first instance from a screenshot; the audit found the other two.

| where | what it did |
|---|---|
| scoring + eligibility (#32, #34) | a sweater at 07:45 for a 34.8° day |
| **the AI re-ranker** (#35) | told the current temperature while the shortlist was built for the peak |
| **the rain rule** (#36) | a 09:00 drop chose suede shoes *underneath a line reading "Rain from 15:00 — take a shell"* |

That last one is my favourite kind of bug: the app warned you about weather it had just dressed you wrongly for.

`lib/weather/planning.ts` is now the single answer to "what weather is this look for?" — one `hoursFor` helper serves both temperature and rain, so they can't drift onto different clocks again.

## The second finding is the one that shows

The model making the final pick could only see **category, subcategory and colours**. So the pattern-clash work only ordered the shortlist — the model chose blind to it — and the "why" was inventing fabric from garment names. Same closet, before and after:

> ~~Black cable knit sweater grounds the look… adds warmth appropriate for the mild weather.~~

> The crisp white **linen** oxford keeps you cool in **29°C** heat while the beige **lyocell** trousers create a soft, monochromatic palette.

Since `CLAUDE.md` calls that sentence the product differentiator *and* the share-card copy, this was worth more than the ranking change.

**One limit I left alone deliberately:** `weatherLabel` is still the condition *now*, so on a clear morning that turns wet the model might write "perfect for the clear day." The wardrobe consequence is already handled and the strip tells you — it's prose only. Noted in `STATE.md` rather than fixed.

## Where that leaves the queue

**Nothing in `todo/` is executable without a decision from you:**

- **#10 `wear-stats`** — blocked on designing what *"unlocks 14 new outfits"* actually simulates.
- **#14 route/URL audit** and **#16 full design audit** — both deliberately run last.

And still open from before, both of which matter more than any remaining plan:

- **Open-Meteo isn't licensed for commercial use** — and after this week it's the backbone of the product.
- **Packing mode is sold in the upgrade sheet and doesn't exist.**

I'd pick the Open-Meteo question next. It's the only thing on the list that can stop you shipping.

2	
3	> **For agentic workers:** REQUIRED SUB-SKILL: Use superpowers:subagent-driven-development (recommended) or superpowers:executing-plans to implement this plan task-by-task. Steps use checkbox (`- [ ]`) syntax for tracking.
4	
5	**Goal:** Build `/stats` — closet value, total wears, average cost per wear, most-worn, gathering-dust, and the gap analysis that tells you which single missing piece would unlock the most outfits.
6	
7	**Architecture:** All of it is aggregation over `items` + `wear_logs`, except the gap analysis, which is a **simulation**: inject a hypothetical garment into the real closet, run the existing candidate builder, and count how many new valid combinations appear. No AI call anywhere on this screen.
8	
9	**Tech Stack:** TypeScript 6, Supabase, Vitest.
10	
11	## Global Constraints
12	
13	- **Depends on** `2026-07-24-outfit-detail-wear-logging.md` (wear data), `2026-07-24-item-data-completeness.md` (prices), and `2026-07-24-seasons-soft-preference.md` (which is where `eligibleByCategory` is created — Task 2 counts slots through it). Without them, five of the six sections are empty.
14	- **TDD, strictly.** Branch: `feat/wear-stats`. No AI attribution.
15	- **No AI calls.** Gap analysis is deterministic — it reuses `buildCandidates`.
16	- Test: `npx vitest run <path>` / `npm run test:run`. Types: `npx tsc --noEmit`. Build: `npm run build`.
17	
18	## Source
19	
20	`design_handoff_stylist_generator/Fitcheck.dc.html:737-780`. Review: `docs/design-review-2026-07-24.md` §6.6.
21	
22	## Explicitly out of scope
23	
24	**"See curated picks"** (`:767`). The design puts a CTA under the gap card that leads to shoppable
25	recommendations — an affiliate or commerce surface with no product, legal or partner decision behind it
26	anywhere in this project. **Do not build it, and do not render a dead button.** The gap card ships
27	without a CTA until that decision exists. Flagging it here so it is not lost.
28	
29	## The gap analysis, stated plainly
30	
31	*"A camel overcoat unlocks 14 new outfits"* is not a query. It is: for each of a fixed set of
32	**archetypal missing pieces**, add it to the user's closet in memory, re-run `buildCandidates` across
33	every occasion, and report the piece with the largest increase in valid combinations.
34	
35	This is honest — the number means exactly what it says, because it is produced by the same code that
36	builds real outfits. It is also bounded: a fixed candidate list times four occasions is a few dozen
37	`buildCandidates` calls over an array already in memory.

46

48

50	import { closetStats, mostWorn, gatheringDust } from "../aggregate";
51	
52	const items = [
53	  { id: "a", price: 100 },
54	  { id: "b", price: 50 },
55	  { id: "c", price: null },
56	];
57	
58	test("closet value sums known prices and ignores unpriced pieces", () => {
59	  expect(closetStats(items, []).value).toBe("£150.00");
60	});
61	
62	test("average cost per wear divides total value by total wears", () => {
63	  const s = closetStats(items, [{ item_id: "a" }, { item_id: "a" }, { item_id: "b" }]);
64	  expect(s.totalWears).toBe(3);
65	  expect(s.avgCostPerWear).toBe("£50.00");
66	});
67	
68	test("no wears means no average, not a division by zero", () => {
69	  expect(closetStats(items, []).avgCostPerWear).toBeNull();
70	});
71	
72	test("an entirely unpriced closet reports zero value and no average", () => {
73	  const s = closetStats([{ id: "c", price: null }], [{ item_id: "c" }]);
74	  expect(s.value).toBe("£0.00");
75	  expect(s.avgCostPerWear).toBeNull();

78	test("most worn ranks by count, highest first", () => {

80	});
81	
82	test("gathering dust surfaces the longest-idle pieces with their age", () => {
83	  const idle = gatheringDust(items, { a: "2026-07-20", b: "2026-01-01" }, "2026-07-24", 2);
84	  expect(idle[0]).toEqual({ id: "b", days: 204 });
85	});
86

89	  expect(idle.map((i) => i.id)).toContain("z");
90	});

content.text:
Design specifies four sections: **headline trio → Most worn → Your biggest gap → Gathering dust** (plus the "See curated picks" CTA, which stays out of scope by the plan's own decision — no product or affiliate decision exists behind it).

Tasks 1 and 2 built all the logic. The screen needs one decision from you.

## Where does the Pro line fall?

You already decided the *principle* twice, and the two existing flags (`analytics`, `gapAnalysis`) suggest whoever wrote #25 expected the line to be drawn somewhere inside this screen rather than around it.

The precedent that matters: **on item detail, the wear tiles are free** — times worn, cost-per-wear, last worn. You confirmed that. The rule there was *a fact about the piece you're looking at is free; the screen that analyses your whole wardrobe is Pro.*

Three ways to apply it:

**A — Facts free, analysis Pro.** A free user opens `/stats` and sees their real closet value, total wears and average cost-per-wear. Most worn, Gathering dust and the gap card are behind the upgrade sheet. Costs nothing to serve, and it's the only option where the pitch is made with *their own numbers* — which is exactly `MONETISATION.md`'s argument: *"they pay for it in month three, once the data is theirs."*

**B — The whole screen is Pro.** The profile row stays tappable and `/stats` renders a locked state. Cleanest story, matches `analytics: false` literally, but a free user never learns what they're missing beyond a feature list they've already seen in the sheet.

**C — Row opens the sheet, screen unreachable.** Cheapest to build. It contradicts #25's stated principle — *"the gated control stays live and tappable; nobody buys a feature they have never reached for"* — so I'd only pick it if you want stats invisible until launch.

**I'd take A**, and I'd hold the gap card behind `gapAnalysis` specifically. It's the most expensive-feeling thing on the screen and the most concrete: *"Grey wool trousers unlock 14 new outfits"* is a sentence worth €5 in a way that "you've worn 47 things" is not. It also means the two flags earn their existence instead of being duplicates.

The cost of A is that free users get a genuinely useful number for nothing. I think that's the point — the same reason the daily drop is free.

Which line do you want?

Task 3 is committed and the screen works. Two findings from the live check that I need you on — both are about the gap card's claim, which is the most expensive-feeling thing on a paid screen.

Measured on your real 21-item closet:

| candidate | unlocks |
|---|---|
| Clean white sneakers | **+258** |
| Brown leather loafers | +198 |
| Dark denim | +129 |
| Grey wool trousers | +99 |
| A navy knit | +72 |
| A white oxford shirt | +54 |
| **A camel overcoat** | **+0** |

## 1. "Unlocks 258 new outfits" is arithmetically true and completely uncredible

Your closet already has 774 buildable combinations across four occasions; sneakers add 33%. The number isn't wrong — it's the same slot arithmetic the generator uses. But nobody believes 258, and the design's own example was **14**. On a paid screen whose whole pitch is honesty, a number that reads as marketing does more damage than a smaller one.

Options: keep the raw count · report one occasion instead of four (≈60) · report the **proportion** ("adds a third more outfits") · re-word to "combinations".

**I'd go with the proportion.** It's scale-free — it reads sensibly on a 20-piece closet and a 200-piece one, where any raw count eventually becomes silly. And "a third more outfits" is a claim you can defend line by line.

## 2. A camel overcoat can never be the answer — the design's own example is unreachable

This one's sharper. `NEUTRAL_WEATHER` is 16°C, and `needsOuterwear` is false above 15°, so **no combination in the simulation ever contains a coat**. Outerwear scores exactly 0 for every user, forever. The plan picked 16° so the recommendation wouldn't swing with the weather — a good instinct that silently killed a whole category.

The fix is to simulate across a cold pass *and* a mild pass, which is what a year of wearing actually looks like. A coat then earns its number on the cold half, and the answer still doesn't change from Tuesday to Thursday.

That makes every number roughly double, which is another argument for reporting a proportion rather than a count.

Both are yours to call: one is copy that makes a promise, the other changes what the app recommends people buy. Want proportion + two-season simulation?

content.text:
Fair challenge — let me actually stress-test it rather than just agree with myself, because my first instinct had a hole in it.

**The objection I had to my own recommendation:** a percentage should get *less* impressive as a closet grows, which is backwards — your paying users have the biggest closets. If Pro subscribers see "+2%", that's an argument against buying anything.

So I checked the maths, and it turns out that's wrong. Adding one piece to a slot of size *s* multiplies the total by (s+1)/s. **The proportion is exactly 1/s — the size of the bottleneck slot — and it's completely independent of every other slot.** Your closet: 3 pairs of shoes, +33%. Exactly ⅓. It only shrinks when *that specific slot* is genuinely deep, which is the honest answer at that point ("you have ten pairs of shoes, another won't do much").

And the decisive one for the future: **the raw count depends entirely on parameters we invented.** Four occasions? Two seasons? Each choice multiplies the number. 258 today, ~516 the moment I add the cold pass — same wardrobe, same truth, double the claim. A number that moves when we change an internal constant is not a number we can defend to a customer. **The proportion is invariant to all of it.**

So yes, it's the right call, and for a better reason than I first gave.

One improvement on top: I'll **lead the card with the bottleneck in your own numbers** — *"3 pairs of shoes against 11 tops"* — because that's the actual finding, it's verifiable by counting, and it's the kind of "why" this app sells. Implementing all three now.

input.new_string:
## Merged (PRs #37, #38) — queue #10, Wear Stats

733 tests · `tsc` clean · `build` clean · lint at main's baseline. Verified against SQL rather than the
screen, and live on an iPhone 17 Pro simulator in BOTH tiers and in the zero-wear state.

**The Pro line is "facts free, analysis Pro"** (user decision, 2026-08-17). A free user sees their own
closet value, total wears and cost-per-wear; Most worn, Gathering dust and the gap card sit behind the
`UpgradeSheet`, **named and tappable** rather than hidden. It mirrors the rule already settled on item
detail, and it is the only shape where the pitch is made with the user's OWN numbers — `MONETISATION.md`'s
whole argument for why anyone pays in month three. `analytics` and `gapAnalysis` gate independently.

### ⚠️ The plan carried three defects against shipped code

Fixed in the plan text before executing, and listed in its own "Amendments" section: it priced
everything in **GBP** (PR #22 shipped `en-IE`/EUR), it would have **re-implemented `daysBetween`**
rather than reusing the DST-safe one, and it had **no Pro gate at all** — it predates PR #25 entirely.

### ⚠️ The gap card was rebuilt THREE times, each against real data

None of these would have been caught by a unit test written from the plan.

1. **"Unlocks 258 new outfits."** Arithmetically exact, wholly uncredible — the design's example was 14.
   And the count scales with parameters we invented (four occasions, two conditions): adding the cold
   pass doubled it overnight for an unchanged wardrobe. **A number that moves when an internal constant
   changes cannot be defended to a customer.** Now a proportional `share`, which depends on the depth of
   the bottleneck slot and nothing else.
2. **A camel overcoat could never be the answer.** The simulation ran at ONE mild temperature and
   `needsOuterwear` is false above 15°, so no simulated combination ever held a coat and every outerwear
   candidate scored exactly 0 — the design's own headline example was unreachable for every user. There
   is now a cold pass, and ⚠️ **outerwear counts as REQUIRED within it**, because a plain slot product
   cannot value the FIRST coat: 0 coats and 1 coat both give one variant, so the most valuable purchase
   a coatless person can make scored nothing.
3. **A wardrobe that can build NOTHING reported "Adds 1% more outfits"** (PR #38). `share` is
   `unlocks / before`, and `before` is zero when a required slot is empty — so going from zero buildable
   outfits to 344 rendered as a rounding error, at the shape a user has straight out of onboarding's
   "capture your first five". `share` is now `null` there and the card says
   *"Your closet can't build a look without one."*

⚠️ **The reason line is phrased about the WINNING candidate's slot, never the smallest slot in the
abstract.** They differ, and the first version recommended a camel overcoat while explaining that shoes
were the problem. `slotCounts` includes Outerwear, which `REQUIRED_CATEGORIES` does not.

**"See curated picks"** (design `:767`) is deliberately absent — a shoppable surface with no product,
legal or partner decision behind it. A test pins its absence.

### Task 4 verification, and how it was done without touching real data

- **Step 2 (the gap sanity-check) is what found defect 3.** Bottoms were stripped **in memory** rather
  than by archiving the real closet — same code path, no writes — and both numbers were re-derived
  independently rather than trusted: full closet 2064 → 2856 (+792, 38%), no-bottoms 0 → 344.
- **Step 3 (the zero-wear state) needed a real write.** The three `wear_logs` rows were temporarily
  reassigned to the other local profile, screenshotted, and **restored byte-identically** — same ids,
  same `outfit_id`s, same dates, verified by query afterwards. ⚠️ An earlier attempt to archive the
  closet's bottoms was refused by the permission layer; that is why Step 2 went the in-memory route.
- **`profiles.tier` was flipped to `free` to photograph the gate, and restored to `pro`.**
- **Local data is unchanged.** Closet prices are all null, so the screen honestly reads €0.00 and hides
  the cost-per-wear tile rather than printing a false average.

content.content:
--- title: Next.js 16.3 description: Next.js 16.3 introduces Instant Navigations, a suite of tools for single-page-app responsiveness, plus a faster dev server, faster builds, and improved tooling for AI agents. url: "https://nextjs.org/blog/next-16-3" docs_index: /docs/llms.txt publishedAt: August 3rd 2026 --- Last month we published a preview release of 16.3 that let you try out [SPA-like navigations](/blog/next-16-3-instant-navigations), better [AI tooling](/blog/next-16-3-ai-improvements), and a _much_ less memory-hungry [dev server](/blog/next-16-3-turbopack). Today, we're excited to announce that Next.js 16.3 is here! This release is packed with improvements for all existing Next.js apps: - [**Less memory usage in dev.**](#less-memory-usage-in-dev) Long dev sessions now use up to 90% less RAM. - [**Faster builds.**](#faster-builds) Repeat builds can read unchanged artifacts from cache. - [**Faster type checking.**](#faster-type-checking-with-typescript-7) `next build` can use TypeScript 7 for type checking. - [**Faster server-side rendering.**](#faster-server-side-rendering) Next.js now handles up to 22% more requests under load. - [**Versioned docs for AI agents.**](#versioned-docs-for-ai-agents) Coding agents read version-matched docs with no setup. - [**Fewer prefetch requests.**](#fewer-prefetch-requests) Links trigger fewer requests by bundling smaller payloads. - [**Better caching for static assets.**](#better-caching-for-static-assets) Immutable assets can optionally be reused across deploys. - [**Custom error boundaries.**](#custom-error-boundaries) Recover from server errors by re-fetching failed data. - [**Built-in glob imports.**](#built-in-glob-imports) Import multiple files with a new Turbopack API. - [**Root params.**](#root-params) Easily access root-level params like `[lang]` from any Server Component. It also includes **Instant Navigations**, an opt-in suite of tools that brings the responsiveness of client-driven SPAs to Next.js, without sacrificing the benefits that come with its server-driven model: - [**Instant Insights.**](#instant-insights) A new devtool that automatically surfaces slow navigations. - [**Partial Prefetching.**](#partial-prefetching) Fine-grained control over how much content a link should prefetch. - [**Better Incremental Static Regeneration.**](#better-incremental-static-regeneration-isr) URLs omitted from build-time prerendering can now serve an instant loading shell to the first visitor. - [**Navigation Inspector.**](#navigation-inspector) A new devtool that lets you visually inspect a navigation's loading shell. - [**Playwright test helper.**](#playwright-test-helper) Write regression tests that prevent refactors from making a navigation slow. The behaviors behind Instant Navigations will become the default in a future major version, as they're part of our work over the last year to simplify Next.js back to its roots: dynamic by default, with no hidden or implicit caching. 16.3 also includes [experimental features](#experimental-features) you can try today, such as the Rust-based React Compiler and network resilience. --- This is our biggest update to the framework since Next.js 16.0 came out last November, and we can't wait for you to try it. Upgrade by installing the latest version of `next` from npm: ```bash filename="terminal" npm install next@latest ``` ...and keep reading to learn about everything that's new! ## Improvements for today's apps Next.js 16.3 includes improvements for all existing projects, including lower dev server memory usage, faster rendering, and better runtime performance, all with zero changes to your application code. We recommend all apps upgrade to 16.3 to start getting these benefits today. ### Less memory usage in dev In 16.3, Turbopack uses **up to 90% less memory** when running `next dev`. The reduction comes from two new features that are now enabled by default: disk caching for dev (first introduced in 16.1), and memory eviction. We've been hearing [great reports](https://github.com/vercel/next.js/discussions/95130#discussioncomment-17439239) from early adopters, and we're excited to bring these performance improvements to all Next apps. Learn more about [Turbopack's new memory eviction features](/docs/app/api-reference/config/next-config-js/turbopackMemoryEviction). ### Faster builds The disk caching feature that's been speeding up dev since 16.1 now works with `next build` and is enabled by default. We've been dogfooding this in production at Vercel for months and are seeing some projects with **5.5x faster builds** on CI. Learn more about setting up [Turbopack's new FileSystem Cache](/docs/app/api-reference/config/next-config-js/turbopackFileSystemCache). ### Faster type checking with TypeScript 7 [Typescript 7](https://devblogs.microsoft.com/typescript/announcing-typescript-7-0/) was released last month, which is a 10x faster native port of TypeScript with much faster type checking. To start using TypeScript 7 for type checking during `next build`, just bump your project's local dependency: ```shell pnpm add -D typescript@^7 ``` Learn more about [configuring TypeScript's CLI in Next.js](/docs/app/api-reference/config/next-config-js/useTypeScriptCli). ### Faster server-side rendering We replaced web streams with native Node.js streams in the App Router rendering layer, removing the overhead of converting between the two during server-side rendering. In our benchmarks, apps handle up to **22% more requests under load**, with no changes to application code. Read the [native Node.js streams PR](https://github.com/vercel/next.js/pull/94311) for more details. ### Versioned docs for AI agents AI coding agents now automatically read documentation that matches your project's version of Next.js. Running `next dev` writes and maintains a version-matched `AGENTS.md` block that points directly to the bundled docs in your project's local node modules. With that knowledge now reaching agents directly, we're retiring [our earlier Skills](https://github.com/vercel-labs/next-skills) that existed solely to bring current documentation to your apps. Learn more about [setting up Next.js for AI coding agents](/docs/app/guides/ai-agents). {/* prettier-ignore */} {/* But Skills are still useful for longer multi-step workflows, and Next.js 16.3 adds several new first-party Skills focused on that work. The [`next-dev-loop`](https://www.skills.sh/vercel/next.js/next-dev-loop) Skill gives your agent a repeatable way to inspect the running app, make an edit, and verify the result using the Next.js dev server and [`agent-browser`](https://github.com/vercel-labs/agent-browser): ```bash filename="terminal" npx skills add vercel/next.js --skill next-dev-loop ``` Read our guide on [setting up Next.js for AI coding agents](/docs/app/guides/ai-agents). For a deeper dive into these AI tooling improvements, read [Next.js 16.3: AI Improvements](/blog/next-16-3-ai-improvements). Later in this post, other Skills build on `next-dev-loop`. \*/} ### Fewer prefetch requests In 16.3, prefetches below a certain payload size are automatically bundled together to reduce the overall amount of prefetch requests your app makes. Prefetches for larger shared segments still remain separate, so they can be reused across multiple routes. Learn more about [prefetch inlining](/docs/app/api-reference/config/next-config-js/prefetchInlining). ### Better caching for static assets Immutable static assets can now be reused across deployments. Since they're immutable, they cannot suffer from issues related to skew. Learn more about [immutable static assets](/docs/app/api-reference/adapters/immutable-static-assets). ### Custom error boundaries Previously, React error boundaries in Next.js interfered with application code that called `notFound` or `redirect`. They also could only reset client-side state, and gave you no way to retry Server Components that failed during rendering. In Next.js 16.3, you can use `catchError` to define a custom error boundary that doesn't interfere with `notFound` or `redirect`: ```tsx filename="app/my-error-boundary.tsx" 'use client'; import { catchError, type ErrorInfo } from 'next/error'; function ErrorFallback(props: { title: string }, { error, retry }: ErrorInfo) { return (

{props.title}

{error.message}

); } export default catchError(ErrorFallback); ``` The boundary also receive a `retry()` function that you can call to refetch the boundary's children, which can include rerendering any Server Components. Learn more about [custom error boundaries](/docs/app/getting-started/error-handling#nested-error-boundaries). ### Built-in glob imports Turbopack now supports loading multiple modules from the file system using the Vite-compatible `import.meta.glob` API, which brings hot-module reloading and other benefits to Server Components that read from local files: ```tsx filename="app/blog/page.tsx" import matter from 'gray-matter'; export default function Page() { // .md needs a loader registered in next.config.js const posts = import.meta.glob('./posts/*.md', { eager: true }); return (
    {Object.entries(posts).map(([path, mod]) => { const { data } = matter(mod.default); return
  • {data.title}
    • ; })}
); } ``` Learn more about [glob imports](/docs/app/api-reference/turbopack#importmetaglob). ### Root params Previously, the only way to access a dynamic route's params was to pass them down as props from the route's page. This led to excessive prop-drilling for params defined above the root layout, which are effectively global and therefore likely to be used throughout your component tree. Next.js 16.3 introduces a new feature for easily accessing these _root params_ from any Server Component, without the need for passing props: ```tsx {1,7} filename="app/[lang]/posts/[slug]/page.tsx" import { lang } from 'next/root-params'; export default async function PostPage( props: PageProps<'/[lang]/posts/[slug]'>, ) { const { slug } = await props.params; const language = await lang(); return (

Language: {language}

Post: {slug}

); } ``` This makes it much more ergonomic for things like internationalization, where many shared utilities and deeply nested components need access to the current language. Additionally, root params also work inside of `use cache` scopes. They're currently supported in Server Components, and we're planning on adding support for route handlers and Server Actions in a future release. Learn more about [root params](/docs/app/api-reference/functions/next-root-params). --- So that's what's new for every app that upgrades today. But 16.3 includes an exciting set of opt-in features that are paving the way for the next major version of the framework, and we're excited to dig into those next. ## Instant Navigations Over the past year, we've been working on fixing the most frustrating things about building with Next.js. Server Components helped apps ship less JavaScript and avoid network waterfalls, but they made navigations feel slow. The caching model was implicit, confusing, and not helpful for dynamic apps. Prefetching was too aggressive and costly. Last November, we introduced a new caching primitive to the framework: the `'use cache'` directive. It's more explicit and composable than our previous server-side caching APIs, and now, it also brings client-side caching to Next.js for the first time. We've been building on this primitive to address the navigation, caching, and prefetching problems above, and we ended up with a simpler, more powerful programming model. Server Components and Suspense are still the two primary building blocks, and `'use cache'` now integrates with them in a way that lets you build apps that are static, dynamic, or _anywhere_ in between. For a deeper dive on these new behaviors, read [last month's announcement of Instant Navigations](/blog/next-16-3-instant-navigations). In 16.3, you can start using building with all these new features by enabling two flags: ```ts filename="next.config.ts" import type { NextConfig } from 'next'; const nextConfig: NextConfig = { cacheComponents: true, partialPrefetching: true, }; export default nextConfig; ``` And if you have existing projects to upgrade, you or your agent can [migrate an app to Cache Components](/docs/app/guides/migrating-to-cache-components). Here's a look at what's getting better in Next.js. ### Instant Insights While Server Components made Next.js apps faster at fetching data and rendering _complete_ pages, apps built with prior versions of Next.js often felt _less responsive_ than their client-driven counterparts (like SPAs), since those apps could render instant loading states without fetching from the server whenever you clicked a link. It was possible to do this using separate `loading.tsx` files for each route, but it was far too easy to forget one and end up with a slow navigation. We've fixed this by letting components that render dynamic UI either define inline loading states with Suspense, or mark part of their UI as prerenderable with `'use cache'`. In either case, Next.js can extract this UI and load it into the client prior to a navigation, making your app feel as snappy as an SPA once users start clicking around it. To ensure you don't miss a slow page, the Next.js DevTools now include **Instant Insights**, which surfaces any navigations you encounter that are not instant: Prefetching that UI ensures your server-rendered app always has _some_ UI ready to show the moment a user clicks a link, similar to how you would model loading states in an SPA. Each insight also provides a prompt that teaches your agent how to apply your chosen fix. Learn more about [Instant Insights](/docs/app/guides/instant-navigation#validate-instant-navigation). ### Partial Prefetching Prior to 16.3, prefetching in Next.js was limiting: you could either define a reusable loading shell with `loading.tsx`, or opt-in to aggressive full-page prefetching with ``. Many apps suffered from these implicit and restrictive APIs, and ended up with blocking navigations on link clicks as a result. To fix this, 16.3 adds a new prefetching behavior we call **Partial Prefetching**. Next.js can extract reusable loading shells from _any_ route's UI, and per-link prefetching via `` can include as much _or as little_ content from the target page as you like. Learn how you or your agent can [adopt Partial Prefetching in your app](/docs/app/guides/adopting-partial-prefetching). ### Better Incremental Static Regeneration (ISR) 16.3 brings a new kind of Incremental Static Regeneration to dynamic, personalized apps. When you prerender only _some_ of a route's pages at build time with `generateStaticParams`, the rest of the page faced a tradeoff. They could show a loading shell but never get prerendered, or skip the shell and block the first visitor. Now you get both. A page you don't prerender serves an instant loading shell on its first visit, then upgrades to the fully prerendered page in the background. Every later visitor gets the final content from the cache. We're also exploring an API to control how often a page upgrades, for example based on traffic. Learn more about [Incremental Static Regeneration with Cache Components](/docs/app/guides/incremental-static-regeneration-cache-components). ### Navigation Inspector Because Next.js disables prefetching in development, it can be hard to understand exactly what a user will see during a particular navigation's loading sequence. The new Navigation Inspector lets you pause page loads and client-side navigations at the shell, so you can see exactly what loading state the user would see: See our documentation on [visualizing loading states with the Next.js DevTools](/docs/app/guides/instant-navigation#visualize-loading-states-with-the-nextjs-devtools). ### Playwright test helper Another common failure mode is a page that navigates instantly today becoming slow tomorrow. Maybe a component that reads `cookies()` gets added to a shared header and de-opts the route to request-time rendering, or a `` boundary moves during a refactor and part of the page starts blocking. Either way, UI that used to appear immediately no longer does. The new `instant()` test helper lets you write Playwright tests that assert exactly what content should be instantly visible during a navigation. The test fails whenever the instant UI changes, no matter the cause: ```ts {7-12} filename="e2e/instant-navigation.spec.ts" import { expect, test } from '@playwright/test'; import { instant } from '@next/playwright'; test('product title is available immediately', async ({ page }) => { await page.goto('/products/shoes'); // Assert what's visible without waiting for network await instant(page, async () => { await page.click('a[href="/products/hats"]'); await expect(page.locator('h1')).toContainText('Baseball Cap'); await expect(page.getByText('Checking inventory...')).toBeVisible(); }); await expect(page.getByText('12 in stock')).toBeVisible(); }); ``` Learn more about [writing tests with the `instant` test helper](/docs/app/guides/instant-navigation#prevent-regressions-with-e2e-tests). --- That's everything that's new with Instant Navigations! We're excited for you to try out these new features and hear what you think. Lastly, there's a few new experimental features shipping with 16.3. ## Experimental features Alongside the stable release, 16.3 ships a few experimental features you can opt into today behind configuration flags. They're still evolving, so let us know how they're working for you in the [Next.js 16.3 feedback discussion](https://github.com/vercel/next.js/discussions/95130). ### Rust-based React Compiler The React Compiler optimizes your components at build time so you don't have to hand-tune memoization. Until now, enabling the React Compiler meant running it through Babel in Node.js. The experimental Rust port instead runs directly inside Turbopack, avoiding the extra work of generating and reparsing code. Enable the compiler and opt into the Rust version in your Next.js config: ```ts filename="next.config.ts" import type { NextConfig } from 'next'; const nextConfig: NextConfig = { reactCompiler: true, experimental: { turbopackRustReactCompiler: true, }, }; export default nextConfig; ``` In tests against large apps like [v0](https://v0.app), the Rust path cut the time from `next dev` to a ready page by 34% on a cold build and 46% on a warm one. These gains assume you've moved off Babel entirely. If you still run Babel for other transforms, the Rust compiler helps, but the gain is smaller. Learn more about [the Rust React Compiler](/docs/app/api-reference/config/next-config-js/turbopackRustReactCompiler). ### Network resilience When the network drops, a soft navigation, data fetch, or Server Action normally throws. --- title: Next.js 16.3 description: Next.js 16.3 introduces Instant Navigations, a suite of tools for single-page-app responsiveness, plus a faster dev server, faster builds, and improved tooling for AI agents. url: "https://nextjs.org/blog/next-16-3" docs_index: /docs/llms.txt publishedAt: August 3rd 2026 --- Last month we published a preview release of 16.3 that let you try out [SPA-like navigations](/blog/next-16-3-instant-navigations), better [AI tooling](/blog/next-16-3-ai-improvements), and a _much_ less memory-hungry [dev server](/blog/next-16-3-turbopack). Today, we're excited to announce that Next.js 16.3 is here! This release is packed with improvements for all existing Next.js apps: - [**Less memory usage in dev.**](#less-memory-usage-in-dev) Long dev sessions now use up to 90% less RAM. - [**Faster builds.**](#faster-builds) Repeat builds can read unchanged artifacts from cache. - [**Faster type checking.**](#faster-type-checking-with-typescript-7) `next build` can use TypeScript 7 for type checking. - [**Faster server-side rendering.**](#faster-server-side-rendering) Next.js now handles up to 22% more requests under load. - [**Versioned docs for AI agents.**](#versioned-docs-for-ai-agents) Coding agents read version-matched docs with no setup. - [**Fewer prefetch requests.**](#fewer-prefetch-requests) Links trigger fewer requests by bundling smaller payloads. - [**Better caching for static assets.**](#better-caching-for-static-assets) Immutable assets can optionally be reused across deploys. - [**Custom error boundaries.**](#custom-error-boundaries) Recover from server errors by re-fetching failed data. - [**Built-in glob imports.**](#built-in-glob-imports) Import multiple files with a new Turbopack API. - [**Root params.**](#root-params) Easily access root-level params like `[lang]` from any Server Component. It also includes **Instant Navigations**, an opt-in suite of tools that brings the responsiveness of client-driven SPAs to Next.js, without sacrificing the benefits that come with its server-driven model: - [**Instant Insights.**](#instant-insights) A new devtool that automatically surfaces slow navigations. - [**Partial Prefetching.**](#partial-prefetching) Fine-grained control over how much content a link should prefetch. - [**Better Incremental Static Regeneration.**](#better-incremental-static-regeneration-isr) URLs omitted from build-time prerendering can now serve an instant loading shell to the first visitor. - [**Navigation Inspector.**](#navigation-inspector) A new devtool that lets you visually inspect a navigation's loading shell. - [**Playwright test helper.**](#playwright-test-helper) Write regression tests that prevent refactors from making a navigation slow. The behaviors behind Instant Navigations will become the default in a future major version, as they're part of our work over the last year to simplify Next.js back to its roots: dynamic by default, with no hidden or implicit caching. 16.3 also includes [experimental features](#experimental-features) you can try today, such as the Rust-based React Compiler and network resilience. --- This is our biggest update to the framework since Next.js 16.0 came out last November, and we can't wait for you to try it. Upgrade by installing the latest version of `next` from npm: ```bash filename="terminal" npm install next@latest ``` ...and keep reading to learn about everything that's new! ## Improvements for today's apps Next.js 16.3 includes improvements for all existing projects, including lower dev server memory usage, faster rendering, and better runtime performance, all with zero changes to your application code. We recommend all apps upgrade to 16.3 to start getting these benefits today. ### Less memory usage in dev In 16.3, Turbopack uses **up to 90% less memory** when running `next dev`. The reduction comes from two new features that are now enabled by default: disk caching for dev (first introduced in 16.1), and memory eviction. We've been hearing [great reports](https://github.com/vercel/next.js/discussions/95130#discussioncomment-17439239) from early adopters, and we're excited to bring these performance improvements to all Next apps. Learn more about [Turbopack's new memory eviction features](/docs/app/api-reference/config/next-config-js/turbopackMemoryEviction). ### Faster builds The disk caching feature that's been speeding up dev since 16.1 now works with `next build` and is enabled by default. We've been dogfooding this in production at Vercel for months and are seeing some projects with **5.5x faster builds** on CI. Learn more about setting up [Turbopack's new FileSystem Cache](/docs/app/api-reference/config/next-config-js/turbopackFileSystemCache). ### Faster type checking with TypeScript 7 [Typescript 7](https://devblogs.microsoft.com/typescript/announcing-typescript-7-0/) was released last month, which is a 10x faster native port of TypeScript with much faster type checking. To start using TypeScript 7 for type checking during `next build`, just bump your project's local dependency: ```shell pnpm add -D typescript@^7 ``` Learn more about [configuring TypeScript's CLI in Next.js](/docs/app/api-reference/config/next-config-js/useTypeScriptCli). ### Faster server-side rendering We replaced web streams with native Node.js streams in the App Router rendering layer, removing the overhead of converting between the two during server-side rendering. In our benchmarks, apps handle up to **22% more requests under load**, with no changes to application code. Read the [native Node.js streams PR](https://github.com/vercel/next.js/pull/94311) for more details. ### Versioned docs for AI agents AI coding agents now automatically read documentation that matches your project's version of Next.js. Running `next dev` writes and maintains a version-matched `AGENTS.md` block that points directly to the bundled docs in your project's local node modules. With that knowledge now reaching agents directly, we're retiring [our earlier Skills](https://github.com/vercel-labs/next-skills) that existed solely to bring current documentation to your apps. Learn more about [setting up Next.js for AI coding agents](/docs/app/guides/ai-agents). {/* prettier-ignore */} {/* But Skills are still useful for longer multi-step workflows, and Next.js 16.3 adds several new first-party Skills focused on that work. The [`next-dev-loop`](https://www.skills.sh/vercel/next.js/next-dev-loop) Skill gives your agent a repeatable way to inspect the running app, make an edit, and verify the result using the Next.js dev server and [`agent-browser`](https://github.com/vercel-labs/agent-browser): ```bash filename="terminal" npx skills add vercel/next.js --skill next-dev-loop ``` Read our guide on [setting up Next.js for AI coding agents](/docs/app/guides/ai-agents). For a deeper dive into these AI tooling improvements, read [Next.js 16.3: AI Improvements](/blog/next-16-3-ai-improvements). Later in this post, other Skills build on `next-dev-loop`. \*/} ### Fewer prefetch requests In 16.3, prefetches below a certain payload size are automatically bundled together to reduce the overall amount of prefetch requests your app makes. Prefetches for larger shared segments still remain separate, so they can be reused across multiple routes. Learn more about [prefetch inlining](/docs/app/api-reference/config/next-config-js/prefetchInlining). ### Better caching for static assets Immutable static assets can now be reused across deployments. Since they're immutable, they cannot suffer from issues related to skew. Learn more about [immutable static assets](/docs/app/api-reference/adapters/immutable-static-assets). ### Custom error boundaries Previously, React error boundaries in Next.js interfered with application code that called `notFound` or `redirect`. They also could only reset client-side state, and gave you no way to retry Server Components that failed during rendering. In Next.js 16.3, you can use `catchError` to define a custom error boundary that doesn't interfere with `notFound` or `redirect`: ```tsx filename="app/my-error-boundary.tsx" 'use client'; import { catchError, type ErrorInfo } from 'next/error'; function ErrorFallback(props: { title: string }, { error, retry }: ErrorInfo) { return (

{props.title}

{error.message}

); } export default catchError(ErrorFallback); ``` The boundary also receive a `retry()` function that you can call to refetch the boundary's children, which can include rerendering any Server Components. Learn more about [custom error boundaries](/docs/app/getting-started/error-handling#nested-error-boundaries). ### Built-in glob imports Turbopack now supports loading multiple modules from the file system using the Vite-compatible `import.meta.glob` API, which brings hot-module reloading and other benefits to Server Components that read from local files: ```tsx filename="app/blog/page.tsx" import matter from 'gray-matter'; export default function Page() { // .md needs a loader registered in next.config.js const posts = import.meta.glob('./posts/*.md', { eager: true }); return (
    {Object.entries(posts).map(([path, mod]) => { const { data } = matter(mod.default); return
  • {data.title}
    • ; })}
); } ``` Learn more about [glob imports](/docs/app/api-reference/turbopack#importmetaglob). ### Root params Previously, the only way to access a dynamic route's params was to pass them down as props from the route's page. Language: {language}

Post: {slug}

); } ``` This makes it much more ergonomic for things like internationalization, where many shared utilities and deeply nested components need access to the current language. They're currently supported in Server Components, and we're planning on adding support for route handlers and Server Actions in a future release. Learn more about [root params](/docs/app/api-reference/functions/next-root-params). --- So that's what's new for every app that upgrades today. Maybe a component that reads `cookies()` gets added to a shared header and de-opts the route to request-time rendering, or a `` boundary moves during a refactor and part of the page starts blocking. Either way, UI that used to appear immediately no longer does. The new `instant()` test helper lets you write Playwright tests that assert exactly what content should be instantly visible during a navigation. The test fails whenever the instant UI changes, no matter the cause: ```ts {7-12} filename="e2e/instant-navigation.spec.ts" import { expect, test } from '@playwright/test'; import { instant } from '@next/playwright'; test('product title is available immediately', async ({ page }) => { await page.goto('/products/shoes'); // Assert what's visible without waiting for network await instant(page, async () => { await page.click('a[href="/products/hats"]'); await expect(page.locator('h1')).toContainText('Baseball Cap'); await expect(page.getByText('Checking inventory...')).toBeVisible(); }); await expect(page.getByText('12 in stock')).toBeVisible(); }); ``` Learn more about [writing tests with the `instant` test helper](/docs/app/guides/instant-navigation#prevent-regressions-with-e2e-tests). --- That's everything that's new with Instant Navigations! We're excited for you to try out these new features and hear what you think. Yes — worth doing, and I've read the release rather than trusting the headline. Here's what it actually buys **Fitcheck** specifically.

**Free, no code change:**
- **~22% more requests under load** — they swapped web streams for native Node streams in App Router SSR. This is the one genuine production win.
- **Fewer prefetch requests** — small prefetches get bundled. Matters for a mobile PWA on cellular more than for most apps.
- **Faster builds** (Turbopack FS cache, now default) and **~90% less dev memory**.
- Immutable static assets reusable across deploys.

**One correction to what you saw:** the headline caching — *Instant Navigations* — is **not** free. It's opt-in behind `cacheComponents: true` + `partialPrefetching: true`, and it's a real architectural change that lands directly on top of **Decision 5**, our daily-drop model. That's a scoped plan, not a flag flip during a version bump. I'd keep it separate.

Two things to note before I touch anything:

1. **`next dev` now writes an `AGENTS.md` block into the repo.** We don't have that file and it isn't gitignored — and this project deliberately keeps meta/authorship docs *out* of git (CLAUDE.md, DESIGN.md, docs/ are all ignored). It'll appear silently after the upgrade, so we should decide where it goes.
2. **TypeScript 7** (10× faster checking) is a separate opt-in — we're on 6.0.3. Own change, own blast radius.

Also worth knowing: our `package.json` says `"next": "^16.2.9"`, so a fresh install on CI could already pull 16.3.x — the lockfile is the only thing holding us at 16.2.9. Doing this deliberately is better than discovering it.

Doing the plain bump now:

input.command: git checkout -q -b chore/next-16-3 && npm install next@16.3.1 eslint-config-next@16.3.1 2>&1 | tail -5; echo "--- installed ---"; npm ls next eslint-config-next 2>/dev/null | grep -E "next@|eslint-config-next@" | head -3
